speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, July 1, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-58, to amend the Criminal Code-Mr. Fulton-Mr. McCleave in the chair.

When the house rose on Wednesday, July 1, we were considering clause 11.
On clause 11-Obscene.
Shall the clause carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the widespread interest in this provision I think it might be helpful if at this stage I give a short statement as to the object and effects of the clause.
The object of this clause is to make a statutory extension of the definition of obscenity so as to make it perfectly clear that the law of obscenity does apply to a certain type of objectionable material that now appears on the newsstands of Canada and is being sold to the young people of our country with impunity.
We believe we have produced a definition which will be capable of application with speed and certainty, by providing a series of simple objective tests in addition to the somewhat vague subjective test which was the only one formerly available. The tests will be: does the publication complained of deal with sex, or sex and one or more of the other subjects named? If so, is this a dominant characteristic? Again, if so, does it exploit these subjects in an undue manner?
We have been careful in working out this definition not to produce a net so wide that it sweeps in borderline cases or cases about Which there may be genuine differences of opinion. In our efforts we have deliberately stopped short of any attempt to outlaw publications concerning which there may be any contention that they have genuine literary, artistic or scientific merit. These works remain to be dealt with under the Hicklin definition, which is not superseded by the new statutory definition.

Criminal Code
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I should put on the record again at this point the Hicklin definition as laid down by Chief Justice Cockburn in the case of Rex. v. Hicklin in 1868, as follows:
-I think the test of obscenity is this, whether the tendency of the matter charged as obscenity is to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences and into whose hands a publication of this sort may fall.
As I have said, it will be appreciated that this is entirely a subjective definition. It will be observed that while the test in the new proposed definition is in the main objective it does, however, contain two terms which require in part a subjective assessment. The first of these is that the characteristic complained of must be a dominant characteristic. As I say, we believe this will cover, without question, the kind of muck on the newsstands against which our main efforts in this definition are directed. But these words will clearly exclude from the definition books otherwise meritorious but containing the occasional passage which, if torn from the context, might be considered objectionable. In other words, in applying our proposed definition the courts must look at the whole work, not just at an isolated passage or passages.
The second requirement is that the manner of dealing with the named subjects must constitute an undue exploitation of them. Here again it will be clear that, for instance, medical textbooks or other books-including novels-in which such subjects are dealt with in an honest fashion are not put in jeopardy by this definition. There must be an undue exploitation. The word "undue" is one with which the courts are familiar as meaning generally something going beyond what men of good will and common sense would normally tolerate. I do not think we need to fear that this is a harsh or unduly restrictive test.
Then I should like to ask hon. members to consider this clause in the light of the new procedure which we are also providing if the bill is approved, for dealing with such obscene publications. The new procedure is what is described as a procedure in rem. It gives a quick and objective method of dealing with the question of whether or not a publication is obscene. I have said that our definition is, in its main nature, objective and so, I believe, will be the new procedure, particularly by reason of the fact that it will not be necessary to lay a charge.
The new procedure provides a quick and relatively simple method of getting the issue before the court, on its merits, of whether or not a particular publication is obscene. In order to do that you do not have to lay a charge against anybody and therefore it is,

as I said, an objective method of having this question disposed of. The new procedure is closely akin to the procedure which has been in effect in the United Kingdom since 1857 and is a procedure, it might be of interest to the committee to know, that the United Kingdom is retaining substantially unaltered in its new obscene publications bill which was introduced into its parliament this year.
I would suggest to hon. members that it is significant that in the United Kingdom, with its well known determination to preserve civil liberties and the liberties of the subject and to avoid anything which might set up, in normal peacetime, government censorship unduly restricting the rights of free expression, they have had since 1857 and are continuing in the bill they have introduced this year this procedure which we are seeking to introduce for the first time. I do not believe we need to be fearful that here in Canada, by providing this objective test and this objective method of procedure, we are doing anything unduly restrictive of freedom of speech, properly understood.
Here, Mr. Chairman, in the definition we have before us and the new procedure which we are recommending to parliament we have made a serious attempt to meet a problem which is very real and urgent in Canada. I can assure hon. members that anyone who may have had occasion to inspect the sort of material taken from Canadian newsstands, where it is being sold with impunity, which has come into the possession of my department, largely as the result of unsolicited correspondence, would agree when I say that it is high time we devised a method of dealing with this type of publication.
I can assure the house further that it is apparent from the discussions I have had with the law enforcement officers of Canada that they feel the present law is not clearly adequate to deal with this type of trash. It is for that reason that we seek an extension of the definition of obscenity, and by the provision of a new method of procedure we hope to enable our law enforcement officers to deal quickly, fairly and objectively with this type of publication.
I should perhaps in conclusion express my appreciation to hon. members who have spoken on this matter before, and who have given me and my departmental officials the benefit of their views and advice. I do not wish to single out any one member particularly, but I think in fairness I should refer to the very constructive speech made last session by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, who placed upon the record some extremely helpful suggestions as to the approach we might follow in

working out a new definition of obscenity and in working out methods of dealing with the problem. I found his remarks extremely constructive and most helpful.
I have just one question. Can the minister tell us whether the United Kingdom rule embraces this show cause system.

Mr. Chairman, I had practically decided not to take part in this debate and to entrust to lawyers the responsibility of amending the Criminal Code. But, after having read that part of the speech made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), as recorded on page 5319 of Hansard of June 30, I began to wonder whether I should not take part in this debate at the present time.
Here is what the Minister of Justice said at the time:
I have observed that most of the discussion thus far in this debate on second reading has been related to the provisions of the bill which deal with the definition of obscenity. I make no criticism of the fact, but I could not fail to note that the matter was treated with some levity, particularly by the hon. members of the Liberal party from the province of Quebec. I am not, of course, suggesting that the definition we have achieved is perfect. It is the best definition that we could achieve; it is an attempt to deal seriously with a serious subject. I think the house will be interested to note, and I think the country will be interested to note, and I think the province of Quebec particularly will be interested to note that members of the Liberal party from the province of Quebec treated this whole thing, with one exception, in an atmosphere of levity. As I say, I make no criticism of that. The hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Eudes) dealt with the matter seriously. The other members of his party from the province of Quebec, where I am aware that this matter is regarded with a great deal of seriousness, dealt with it as a subject deserving nothing but laughter.
Later on, the Minister of Justice added:
What I say hits my honourable friends a little hard but they recognize that their attitude towards this bill to-night has not done them credit-
And later on, he added again:
My whole purpose in this debate has been to advance the bill along into committee so that we might hear what constructive suggestions my hon. friends have to offer, because certainly their attitude so far has been far from constructive.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that attitude on the part of the Minister of Justice is rather that of a person who would have had us believe that the government had intended to cure all the evil and who, realizing that, having done so little, he must resort to attacks against those who had taken the floor.
I agree with him that the hon. member for Hochelaga made a very serious and documented speech, a speech which deserves to attract general attention. I agree that the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis), who 66968-9-350

is a jovial person by nature, has made, in reference to firearms, some rather amusing remarks, but when he referred to obscenity, he did so with the same seriousness shown by the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice has no reason to claim that the Liberals of the province of Quebec lack any seriousness when a question of morals or manners is involved; and it is in that connection, our duty to point out to him the defects of his own bill.
Besides, we are not the only people who find his bill, although slightly an improvement, falling short of a full victory against obscenity.
On June 17, the Protestant clergy, meeting in London, as reported in the following article, stated:
(Text):
Proposed federal legislation defining obscenity in relation to literature was attacked today by three clergymen here for the eleventh annual summer school of religion as indefinite and unnecessary.
In an interview at the University of Western Ontario, Dr. James T. Cleland of Duke University, N.C., Rev. W. B. J. Martin of the Scottish Congregational College, Edinburgh, and Rev. D. R. Fraser of Byron, Unitarian Minister in London, agreed a wrong tack was being taken.

The clergymen pointed to the words "dominant" and "undue exploitation" as providing ready made loopholes.

As the minister can see, we are not the only ones to criticize his attitude and, besides, we have good reasons for criticizing, because the minister himself had promised a great deal more than he is giving us now.
There is no doubt that all the members of this house deplore the fact that so many obscene publications are being offered for sale; all of them would like these obscene publications to disappear. But, when the minister addressed the Sacred Heart League, in Montreal, he proposed four changes. First, as is reported in the Gazette of June 14, 1958, here is what the minister said:
(Text):
The first Is a "practical" definition of the word obscene for article 150 of the Criminal Code.
(Translation):
That is just where we take issue with the minister. That definition he gave, which

Criminal Code
includes the words "dominant characteristics" constitutes the dominant part of his bill. Those words are not sufficient to ensure the elimination of those things. We believe that all they do is to enable defence counsels to find easier ways to secure acquittals of the person charged.
Besides, I have talked with some religious authorities and I even had correspondence about that matter. I recalled having answered a letter about this from Mgr. J. N. Gelineau, vicar general of the Ottawa diocese, on June 24, 1959. Here is what I wrote to him:
Monsignor,
I have received your letter dated June 22, as well as the article which appeared in last night's be Droit.
As I was telling you, the major difficulty in finding a complete definition for the word obscenity is that Protestant elements who believe in free will, are convinced, probably with sincerity, that it would interfere with freedom of conscience. It is for that reason that the definition that is given in the amendment to Sections 150, 8 and 150A, far from improving the situation, makes it worse, since it says:
"(8) For the purposes of this Act, any publication the dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex-"
Dominant characteristic may include many things that the judges might consider insufficient to be reproved.
Let me cite an instance that will probably never occur. If, in advertising the comfort of an hotel, a pamphlet showed a man and a woman, in indecent attire, sharing the same bed, the judge might say that this was not the main characteristic of the pamphlet. Yet, the said hotel would appeal to people's evil instincts.
As a matter of fact, section 150A confers the whole responsibility upon the judge who will decide whether the publication or illustrated story is to be classified as obscene or not. Everything is therefore left to the discretion of the judge who may, sincerely or not, have opinions very different from those of Catholic religious authorities.
All I see in this act is a chance for lawyers to win their defence cases more easily.
I am sorry to say that I do not entirely agree with Father Gay who seems to think that the bill is a considerable progress in the fight against obscene magazines.
I do not want to blame Hon. E. Davie Fulton, Minister of Justice, too severely because I know he was working under extremely difficult conditions. What I am condemning, however, is leading the population to believe that a remedy is being provided, whereas nothing of the kind is being done.
Mr. Chairman, that is how we have dealt with the problem from the start. And the Minister of Justice said that we were considering it lightly. We are not dealing lightly with this matter. On the contrary, we are aware of its difficulties.
I remember a banquet where the Minister of Justice was the guest speaker and dealt with the matter of obscenity and of the amendments he proposed to introduce. I also remember having told him that evening that

he would run into extraordinary difficulties because attempts have been made for the past two thousand years to establish a concrete definition of obscenity, and it has not been done yet, because there often is only a very small margin between art and obscenity. I have personally had occasion to see things which would appear obscene to some people, but not so to others, depending on the state of mind of the person who sees or examines or studies those things.
As a matter of fact, some works may be considered obscene by some people and not so by others. When art is mixed with the question of obscenity, the problem becomes more difficult. It is recognized that the dividing line between art and obscenity is sometimes difficult to appreciate. My reproach to the minister is that he has provided an incomplete definition. The minister wanted people all over the country to believe that he was going to make such radical changes that the Criminal Code would scarcely be recognizable with regard to obscenity and obscene publications in this country.

Finally, Fulton said, "we are considering the possibility of including the printers of obscene publications in prosecutions, much more than is done today."
Cardinal Leger, in a 5000-word speech, said-
The printing is bad, but it is not of importance.

The important part is this: the Minister of Justice had promised to find a way to cause the arrest of the printer of such literature, and to take him to court, so as to prevent publication of such obscene works. It was not the first time that the Minister

of Justice came out in favour of taking court action against printers or publishers. In fact, in 1955, as recorded on page 5275 of Hansard, the Minister of Justice, who was then sitting on this side of the house, made the following statement:
-a prosecution should also be required against the printer and publisher if the printer and publisher are in Canada, or against the initial distributor if it be one of those publications which is brought into Canada having been printed in the United States and then distributed in Canada in its finished form.
A little farther down, the minister added:
-and the person most responsible for the offence -that is, the man who first put it into circulation- would be bound to be proceeded against.
Still a little further down, the minister went on to say, and I quote from page 5276 of Hansard:
Another line of attack on the problem, which has been suggested before and rejected but which I would ask the minister to consider again, is that it might be provided that the penalties against printers and publishers, or against those who first put this offensive material into circulation, should be made specific.
Still farther down, the minister had this to say:
They wrote a specific clause into their legislation prohibiting the importation of the plates from which these things are printed. I recommend to the minister that he and the department should give very earnest consideration to whether it would not be desirable to incorporate a similar provision in our Criminal Code.
And the minister went on to say:
I know you cannot increase an unlimited fine, but I was suggesting a minimum fine or a minimum penalty for printers and publishers.
It is in that respect that we are blaming the minister. He had promised us the moon; now it is just a case of the elephant bringing forth a mouse. There have been claims that this constitutes a great improvement. Well, Mr. Chairman, I think if it is an improvement, it is no more than -J, or at most 4 of what it should be. We do recognize that section 12, paragraph 150A contains something new. The provisions of this section make it easier to resort to court action and seizure in the case of obscene literature. Apart from that, I think the minister has tried to build up his political capital by running around the country, and particularly the province of Quebec, to give the impression that, after he had tried to define the word obscenity and had amended the Criminal Code accordingly, everything would be fine.
So, by casting aspersions on Liberal members from Quebec he has attempted, up to a point, to have Canada, and more particularly the province of Quebec, believe that Liberal members are less interested than he in improving the country's morals.

Mr. Chairman, I say to the minister that he should not indulge in petty politics and make speeches such as the one he made on June 30 last. On the contrary, he should show some statesmanship and really try to improve conditions.
We recognize that it is no easy task to define obscenity in a truly concrete and perfect way, because we know the situation is extremely difficult; it has been going on for years, and the minister is not the only one responsible in the matter. However, there should be no petty politics about such an important matter. I therefore ask the minister at this time not to be silly and use words such as those he used on June 30 last when addressing Liberal members who are just as interested as he is in raising Canada's moral standards. We hope the minister will stop making political hay with this question, and will tackle the problem in statesmanlike fashion.

Mr. Chairman, like all right-minded Canadians, I am happy to commend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) for the bill he is submitting today as a means of fighting obscenity, one of the worst forms of degradation that individuals and nations can fall into.
I know that the minister has always been interested in this subject and has closely studied this infinitely delicate and serious problem of obscene literature. He took up this cause many years ago, and today, as Minister of Justice, he wants to give this country legislation that will clean up the newsstands, thus helping society by preventing the sale of evil literature on a national scale.
It is one of those bills which almost automatically call for unanimity. All of us want to bring about the necessary changes.
According to section 150 of the Canadian criminal code, obscenity is a crime leading to severe punishment. But, experts in the field -law enforcement officers, lawyers, judges, social workers-are all agreed that the language of the law is not sufficiently explicit. Then there is always the difficulty attending the onus of the proof, which takes time and money. In fact, obscene publications or shows are only one of the many facets of public immorality which is so brazenly flaunted nowadays.
It is not a new problem, even though it seems to be a characteristic vice of so-called advanced civilizations. We are therefore not facing a new difficulty, a by-product of

Criminal Code
the last war or of scientific progress. But this very progress, the wonders of printing, radio and television, are helping scatter the accursed seed and spread havoc. So, as the allied chiefs used to say during the last war, desperate ills call for desperate remedies. And that remedy is the remoralization of individuals and peoples. Quid leges sine moribus? Yes: what good would laws be without morals? But, men being what they are, we must use drastic measures and cause the iron hand of the law to weigh against all offenders. That is what the government, through the Minister of Justice, is doing today.
According to those who specialize in such delicate problems, we need a clearer definition of obscenity. I think that, under the circumstances, the Minister of Justice is introducing a bill which, though it may not be perfect-there is nothing perfect in this world-represents a great improvement over what we had in the past. I know that the Minister of Justice has drawn upon the many briefs submitted to him, by Catholics, Protestants and Jewish groups as well as all other religious denominations in this country, and I also know that he did not ignore suggestions made to him by Rev. Father Gay who has made a searching study of the matter and suggested a new wording for section 150 of the Criminal Code. Anybody wishing to obtain fuller information with regard to the new wording of that section, need only refer to the newspaper Le Droit of February 23, 1959, which says:
Diocesan press service planned.
A definition of obscenity.
Definition of obscenity submitted by Reverend Father Gay.
However, what really counts is the training of individual conscience and of people's minds. I shall take the liberty of reporting a fact that is perhaps little known but significant. Some time ago, when the Montreal police decided to clean up shows in night clubs, the chief of police called in night club owners and representatives of their employees and told them in substance: "In future, dancing girls will have to conform to the following rules: they must always wear such and such garments; and they must actually dance, and refrain from speaking to patrons. If they can't do that, let them get off the stage and go wash the dishes."
And do you know, Mr. Chairman, that many of those club owners, employees and

even dancers commended the chief of police for doing his utmost to raise the standards of entertainment? Even people directly concerned feel there is nothing to be gained in immorality, and detective lieutenant Lu-cien Quintal, who is in charge of the squad responsible for keeping watch on the decency of shows and publications, has very much less trouble now. Why? Because the police have decided, not to discuss the quality of shows, but to close those which are not up to standards set and adopted both by the police and the show promoters.
Mr. Chairman, we should do the same thing about obscenity. Untold harm is being done to our young people by books and publications, magazines, films, photographs, etc.
Obscenity, violence, unbridled passions, glorification of crime and criminals, those are the many problems leading some of our people to prison. We talk about the rehabilitation of criminals, but it would be much better if we prevented them from becoming criminals. All the pompous terms used by self-styled artists and art critics, the obscure and ambiguous vocabulary of so-called psychiatrists often have but a single carefully disguised purpose: allow immorality to display itself under its more pernicious and degrading forms. That is what we have to fight against.
The problem of immorality and obscene publications is not new, Mr. Chairman, and it is not peculiar to this country either. The Canadian authorities have realized its gravity for a long time, together with other national leaders. As evidence of that, may I refer to the protocols signed in Paris on May 4, 1910, on the repression of the distribution of obscene publications, an agreement which was amended at Lake Success on May 4, 1949, and which has been in force in our country since then.
You will also recall the convention for the repression of the distribution and traffic of obscene publications, signed in Geneva on September 12, 1923, which was amended by a protocol at Lake Success on November 12, 1947, and signed by Canada on November 24 of the same year, at which date it went into force in our country.
If we find it worthwhile to sign international agreements directed against demoralization and obscenity, we should at least be consistent and apply, within our own

borders, the provisions to which we are pledged by those protocols and agreements.
We are committing the serious mistake of believing that the fight against obscenity or immorality is the doing of a mere handful of bilious and scrupulous minds. On the contrary, the Minister of Justice has received testimonies of encouragement from all quarters in Canada, from workers, professionals, students and even from the clergy. Whether we are Catholics, Protestants or Jews, we are not alone. Cardinals and other bishops are not alone, the protestant hierarchy, the rabbis, the most prominent members of the clergy want to see the end of this plague gnawing at the heart of our society.
But it is the responsibility of hon. members of the house to provide the police and the courts with the weapons that they will use efficiently in their fight against that filthy monster which is popular immorality. Most of us here have dependents and we do not want our sons and daughters to be sullied by that infamous literature and those disgusting shows. It is our responsibility to act, and that responsibility is sacred before God and before man.
Mr. Chairman, before closing my remarks, I should like to commend the Knights of Columbus of the province of Quebec who have espoused the fight against obscene literature. Particularly in the diocese of Joliette, at the request of His Excellent Mgr. Papineau, a committee has been formed to fight against obscene literature. That committee, whose action extends over the whole diocese, includes diocesan associations like the Knights of Columbus, the Knights of Champlain and the service clubs of Joliette. They have joined together in waging war against evil literature and in protecting our young people. I want to point out the important work that is being done in that field by the Knights of Columbus of Joliette, Council No. 1468, as well as by Knights of Columbus councils at Ste. Helene de Valois, Montcalm, St. Lin des Laurentides, and L'Assomption. All have done and are still doing much in the fight against obscene literature.
Mr. Chairman, may I once again congratulate the Minister of Justice for rising to his responsibilities, for amending the code in order to rid the nation of evil literature. Of course, there will be criticism of what he is doing, but nothing is perfect in this world, not even this bill. This legislation is not perfect but, even if it were, there would always be someone to try and find loopholes in it. Mr. Chairman, this legislation will be of great help to the Protestant, Jewish
Criminal Code
and Catholic associations, and to all right-minded people of this country by enabling them to fight even more efficiently against evil literature. It gives solid encouragement to law enforcement officers, to judges and to right-minded people across the country to persevere in their attempts to purge Canadian morals.
I commend the Minister of Justice for rising to his responsibility, and for tackling this problem-in fact, he has been at it for many years-and now that he holds the office of Minister of Justice, he is trying to carry out his great desire, that of helping the whole community, in short, to protect the young people of Canada.

The minister is responsible both for this and for another bit of legislation due to come before the house, each of which introduces, at least in my opinion, something completely new, or a new concept in the question of prosecution and the position of a defendant.
I think I can make the point by reading something the minister elaborated in his speech to the Quebec union of municipalities on May 17, 1958. I might point out that what I read also makes nonsense of the suggestion that the minister is not prepared to have any consultations now or to hear any other groups in respect to changes in this code. The minister said:
We have, as I have said before, received some extremely interesting and often very practical suggestions to help us with our problem. A most interesting letter was received from one resident of Ottawa, who gave us his definition of the word obscene:
"Any literature, any spectacle or other matter which you would not like to see related to your mother, or your wife, or young sister, or your daughter."
The correspondent went on to remark that this was plain language that every man could understand. As you can easily see, however, a definition of this type leaves so much open to opinion that it would not seem, at present, to be the practical solution to the law.
Another very excellent suggestion is that the code should prohibit the publication and distribution of material-
And note these words-which the minister said over a year ago; because, as a matter of fact, these are familiar words:
-the dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex, crime, immorality, horror, cruelty or violence, or any one or more of such subjects. This type of definition would appear to be very close to the solution to deal with the type of publication I have referred to a minute ago.
Let me interject here that the minister was very close to the solution last May. Why

Criminal Code
did he have to wait so long to bring it in and deny one group that wanted to make representations the opportunity of doing so?

The minister went on to say:
Then, too, as of recent date, the unique suggestion has come in England recently. There, a policeman or law enforcement officer may seize publications from a newsstand; if he considers them harmful, he can take them to the court. The court then summons the vendor-
This is the key point. I continue:
-and unless he can establish the innocence of the reading material, it is destroyed. If the material is not considered by the court to be obscene the material is then restored to the vendor. This is, perhaps, the most far-reaching method that I have heard of to date, and does place the traditional onus on the defendant rather than on the crown to prove whether or not a publication is obscene.
Does the minister admit that he has gone along with this and is changing the traditional onus which has rested on the crown and placing it on the defendant? I would certainly judge that to be the case from reading clause 12, which states:
12. The said act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 150 thereof, the following sections;
"150a. (1) A judge who is satisfied by information upon oath that there are reasonable grounds for believing that any publication, copies of which are kept for sale or distribution in premises within the jurisdiction of the court, is obscene or a crime comic, shall issue a warrant under his hand authorizing seizure of the copies.
Apparently this places the traditional onus on the defendant rather than on the crown to prove whether or not a publication is obscene. I suggest that if the minister had a reservation a year ago he should still have it now.

This would be dangerous even if we had only one example, but in other legislation the minister has indicated he is bringing in referring to the Combines Investigation Act the same idea is incorporated, and the defendants are going to have to show that there is something good or worth while about their particular monopoly; then they will get off. I am suggesting that these are two changes of which we should be wary because they introduce, as the minister says, a shift in the traditional onus from the crown to the defendant.
To support my contention that the minister's explanation is most unsatisfactory I will read an excerpt from the Ottawa Citizen of March 6, 1959, which reads:
More judicial guidance on what constitutes obscene literature would be helpful to the customs and excise department, deputy minister David Sim said Thursday.
Mr. Sim told the commons estimates committee that he would like to see more appeals to the courts on decisions of the department to ban certain foreign books.
"This way, we would get some direction on this thing," Mr. Sim smiled.
He said that officers of his department and revenue minister Nowlan did not relish their job of acting as censors.
"No one in his right mind would ask for a job like that," he commented.
In my remarks the other evening I pointed out that the main problem in so far as obscene literature or books are concerned lies with publishing that is done outside of Canada. Very little publishing is done in Canada, and such a minimal fraction of that is likely to be obscene that it is obvious that the main problem in so far as rational adults who read are concerned stems from books published outside of Canada, especially in France and perhaps in England and the United States. Perhaps, however, the minister does not agree with me. What does the legislation do in this regard? I gather not a thing except this one point, and I would imagine this could be a dangerous point and I want an explanation from the minister on it.
Under this bill, as I understand it, if a judge does decide something is obscene then notice goes to the attorney general of the province, who I gather can declare that this particular material is obscene as far as that province is concerned. Does this mean that our customs and excise authorities are going to take the decision of the attorney general of one province and apply it all across Canada? I can certainly foresee difficulties arising from

this situation, because there are marked disagreements from province to province about what may constitute an obscene publication.
If as a result of this new procedure the decision of a judge promulgated by an attorney general is to be taken by the customs branch as official advice that will determine whether a book is admitted or barred from a country, we are going to be up against the problem of having the action of one magistrate and one attorney general determining the policy in so far as the importing of certain books is concerned.
The minister indicated that despite the new definition the Hicklin definition of obscenity as something tending to deprave and corrupt would still be enforced. I should like him to give us an indication how he thinks that definition will work. He used a British example, but I wish to point out to him that there has been considerable controversy over the Hicklin definition and over the way United Kingdom censorship is exerted. The objections concentrate largely upon the stage plays and the role of the chamberlain; however, there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction concerning the censorship of books in that country. I can give the minister several examples such as "Lolita", which we can buy in this country because it is allowed in but which is not allowed into England at the present time. Another example is D. H. Lawrence's "Rainbow" away back in 1915, which was barred at one time but later allowed to come in.
The British in their application of the Hicklin ruling regarding depravity and corruption have scared the wits out of many publishers. And England is not looked upon by publishers as being as open and fair a place to publish as is even the United States. The whole question of how you define obscenity, I think we all agree, is most difficult. The meaning of the word "obscenity" as legally defined by the courts in the United States is as follows:
-tending to stir the sex impulses or to lead to sexually impure and lustful thoughts.
This definition is taken from the judgment of John M. Woolsey, United States district judge, in the case of the United States of America v. one book called "Ulysses". The judge went on to say:
Whether a particular book would tend to excite such impulses and thoughts must be tested by the court's opinion as to its effect on a person with average sex instincts-what the French would call Vhomme moyen sensuel-who plays, in this branch of legal inquiry, the same role of hypothetical reagent as does the "reasonable man" in the law of torts and "the man learned in the art" on questions of invention in patent law.
The risk involved in the use of such a reagent arises from the inherent tendency of the trier of facts, however fair he may intend to be, to make
Criminal Code
his reagent too much subservient to his own idiosyncrasies. Here, I have attempted to avoid this, if possible, and to make my reagent herein more objective than he might otherwise be, by adopting the following course:
After I had made my decision in regard to the aspect of "Ulysses", now under consideration, I checked my impressions with two friends of mine who in my opinion answered to the above stated requirement for my reagent.
These literary assessors-as I might properly describe them-were called on separately, and neither knew that I was consulting the other. They are men whose opinion on literature and on life I value most highly. They had both read "Ulysses", and, of course, were wholly unconnected with this cause.
Without letting either of my assessors know what my decision was, I gave to each of them the legal definition of obscene and asked each whether in his opinion "Ulysses" was obscene within that definition.
I was interested to find that they both agreed with my opinion: that reading "Ulysses" in its entirety, as a book must be read on such a test as this, did not tend to excite sexual impulses or lustful thoughts but that its net effect on them was only that of a somewhat tragic and very powerful commentary on the inner lives of men and women.
I bring up that point of literary assessment because of its relevance to the amendment we plan to move to the particular amendment brought in by the minister.
The hon. member for Hull pointed out that some religious groups have protested against the definition contained in this amendment. These religious groups have tended to be, as I understand it from the two items in the newspaper which I noticed, protestant religious groups. This underlines another very touchy and difficult point, that different religious groups have different sensitivity toward censorship and the whole idea of censorship and of obscenity. This is all the more reason why we should be very careful in the kind of measures we introduce.
It is very difficult for me to see how one can bring in an amendment to point out the traditional onus being shifted from the crown to the defendant. I do think that because this is such a switch we deserve a much more careful and reasoned explanation on the part of the minister as to whether it is a desirable thing that is being introduced, and whether it may not put far too much power in the hands of the crown. I know the minister underlined several times that this is designed to get after the comic books and the things that are on the newsstands, but how can he be sure it will not extend farther than that, and that an occasion will not rise when through one magistrate and one attorney general we might find ourselves in a position where much more than just the degrading comic books are in danger of being swept away from people who might care to read them.

Criminal Code
The standards of magistrates will vary from person to person and place to place. I always remember one of the conclusions that Kinsey came to in his study of the sexual habits of the American male, which was I think a very relevant one, that magistrates and lawyers tend to come from a more sophisticated level of society, and certainly a more educated level, than the ordinary working man. They have different mores in regard to certain sexual aberrations. For example, the magistrates and the lawyers and the crown counsel tended to take a much more serious view of rape than the working man or the working class people tended to take. On the other hand, the working class people tended to take a much more serious view of homosexuality than the magistrates and the middle class did.
Kinsey pointed out that this is one of the great difficulties in trying any criminal matters in this particular field. I should like to give the reason for changing the article "a" to "the". First, it seems to me confusing. I would like to understand why a thing has a dominant characteristic. If you say that in a household the wife is the dominant person, that is the dominant characteristic perhaps in that household. "Dominant characteristic" is what confuses me. The only thing I can see it means is that in a book you could have a whole host of dominant characteristics, and you could pinpoint this one. If you take a book like "The Naked and the Dead" by Norman Mailer, which I thought was one of the great commentaries upon the war, to me the dominant characteristic in that book was the fight between the liberals with a small "1" and the fascists represented by the lieutenant and the general.
I could certainly say that was the main theme running through the book. Another reader might look at it and say the dominant characteristic was that of sex, because there were some scenes in it dealing with sex and therefore that would come under consideration. He could say, "Look, I can show this has literary merit because professor so-and-so of Carleton college has said so". Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make on this question because a number of my constituents have been most interested in this legislation. First of all, let me say we all know this matter has been of serious concern to a large number of people throughout Canada in recent years. I want to say right now that we agree with the intentions and objectives of the minister, but I rise to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur because we believe this amendment will further protect the rights of a free press and the right of free speech as we understand it.
As I said before, this is a most difficult problem. I know that so far as our group is concerned, since this legislation was introduced we have given considerable thought to this clause. We have had a number of meetings, and we have discussed the clause from every angle. I can assure the minister it is the intention of this group to offer this amendment in a constructive way in order to best meet his objectives and his intentions.
Now, Mr. Chairman, to indicate that there is serious consideration being given to this legislation since it was introduced into the house, I should like to read a news item from the Gazette of June 17, 1959, which I think puts briefly and in better form than I could the arguments against the clause as it is now worded. The article is entitled, "Clergy Hit Obscene Law Plan". It reads as follows:
Proposed federal legislation defining obscenity in relation to literature was attacked today by three clergymen here for the eleventh annual summer school of religion as indefinite and unnecessary.
In an interview at the University of Western Ontario, Dr. James T. Cleland of Duke University, N.C., Rev. W. B. J. Martin of the Scottish Congregational College, Edinburgh, and Rev. D. R. Fraser of Byron, Unitarian minister in London, agreed a wrong tack was being taken.
"You cannot legislate people into the kinds of individuals they should be," said Mr. Fraser, whose letter to the editor of a London newspaper prompted the discussion.
The letter stated in seeking more information about the proposed legislation: "We are already shackled by the legal chains of an outmoded Victorian morality in such matters as divorce and birth control. Citizens should be on guard to see that the prudery of a few does not place undue hardship or false propriety upon the many."
The reduction of obscenity in Canadian publications might be better achieved by a program of education rather than one of legislation, the ministers maintained.
We heartily agree with that contention. In the long run it is a program of education and of the raising of standards and concepts in this field that will bring the real improvement that we are all seeking.

Wording Has Loopholes
Besides, Dr. Cleland, said, the legislation proposed leaves the matter wide open by its wording. The lawyers will have a field day with it.
We were under that impression, Mr. Chairman, when we were discussing this matter in our caucus. In our opinion it is wide open and leaves opportunities for wide differences of opinion between lawyers, magistrates and judges across Canada.
The legislation defining obscenity planned by justice minister Fulton for inclusion in the Canadian Criminal Code reads: "Any publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex, or of sex and any one or more of the following subjects, namely, crime, horror, cruelty and violence, shall be deemed to be obscene."
The clergymen pointed to the words "dominant" and "undue exploitation" as providing ready made loopholes.
We agree with that contention.
Dr. Cleland and Mr. Martin are guest lecturers at the UWO summer school which is now in its second day at university college.
More than one hundred clergymen are attending the five-day school.
Then to follow up that matter I want to read an editorial from the Globe and Mail of June 15 of this year. It is a very well known paper which generally supports the Conservative line of politics. It is a very fine paper, one which has a very good format and which in my opinion generally has a very excellent and democratic approach to international and national affairs and problems. I read many of the editorials with a great deal of pleasure and agree with them on many occasions, as I do with this one which is entitled "What is Obscenity?". It reads as follows:
Efforts by legislators and courts to define obscenity in literature have never been very successful. The dominion cabinet has just made a creditable attempt in an amendment to the Criminal Code introduced in the House of Commons.
Although the Criminal Code makes it an offence to sell "any obscene written matter, picture, model, phonograph record or other thing whatsoever", it does not at present specify what obscenity is. Police and courts are left to supply their own definitions, with such help as they can obtain from past precedents. The test commonly used in Canada was formulated by an English judge in 1868; "Whether the tendency of the matter charged as obscenity is to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences and into whose hands a publication of this sort may fall".
This definition is open to serious criticism, in that it makes the reactions of immature or abnormal individuals rather than those of normal adults-
Like members of parliament.
-the touchstone for determining whether a book is or is not obscene. Applied rigidly and literally, it can lead to the banning of many serious works of literature.
In place of this old rule, the proposed amendment offers a new definition for obscene matter:

Criminal Code
Then the editorial quotes the section with which we are dealing, namely section 11, and continues:
This is a distinct improvement on the 1868 rule in two particulars.
We agree with that statement.
It lays stress on the "dominant characteristic" of the work rather than on isolated passages. More important, it makes the test whether there has or has not been a deliberate effort to exploit sexual desires. With this definition, it should be a little easier to draw a distinction between real pornography and works with a serious literary purpose.
Even so, the interpretation of the section is bound to present many difficulties. Where, for example, is the line to be drawn between "due" and "undue" exploitation? Narrowly construed, the new definition could condemn such classics as Hamlet, Othello and King Lear, all of which concerned with "sex, crime, horror, cruelty and violence". A great deal will still depend on the good sense of individual judges and magistrates.
It is unfortunate that when the government is trying to bring the law up to date on this matter, it has failed to touch the silliest and most indefensible anomaly of all. This is the rule which gives the Department of National Revenue authority to exclude from Canada any imported material its officials consider immoral or indecent. It is generally agreed that customs inspectors are not qualified to decide-as a sideline to their regular jobs- the often difficult and subtle question of whether a particular book is obscene. They do not, in fact, want the responsibility.
I am sure the Minister of National Revenue has indicated to the house very clearly that he does not enjoy this responsibility.
The law should be changed to leave the decision in all cases to the courts.
We think that editorial has placed the position very well indeed. With respect to the question of what is obscenity, may I say that I listened to a television broadcast at 10.30 p.m. eastern standard time over the trans-Canada network on Wednesday, February 10. I am going to read only the concluding paragraph because I think it deals effectively with the difficulty of definition.
To obviate this and other dangers-
This is referring to obscenity.
-it would seem that the most desirable procedure to deal with the present problem in Canada would be to attempt to enact a satisfactory and workable definition of the term "obscenity" and to apply the law where it was needed. Whether such a definition is possible is a question for those skilled in the law to decide. But this method would certainly seem preferable to the establishment of local or provincial boards of censors or the continuance of the present admittedly inadequate inspection of books entering the country. A combination of the threat of legal action, based on objective criteria, and the pressure of intelligently exerted public opinion should be sufficient to check the spread of unpleasant written material in this country.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, we fully recognize the difficulty of this problem. In moving
66968-9-351i
this amendment we are trying to overcome what we think are some of the objections to the section as it now stands and to make the law clearer for magistrates and judges who have to administer it.
The hon. member for Port Arthur mentioned the different standards of magistrates and judges throughout Canada. I am sure the minister, with his knowledge of British Columbia, realizes that there is a great difference in standards as between magistrates and that things must be clearly defined if the law is going to be fairly applied all across Canada.
In order to illustrate that point may I say this. I remember two old justices of the peace in my district who were good citizens throughout the years. I remember that they always confiscated whisky that was produced in court. When people were charged with drinking it, they would solemnly confiscate it in the name of the crown to be presented to the local hospital. I was president or director of our local hospital for 18 years and I never had knowledge of a drop of that whisky ever turning up at the hospital. I want to mention that the point which always struck me was that the dear old gentleman, who was highly respected and was of Scottish descent, always concluded his sentence, whatever it was, $5 or $50, by saying, "Gentlemen, it is obscene to drink in public." There we have a definition of obscenity, and an example of the difficulties you get into with respect to differences between magistrates and judges. That might be an extreme case, but there is that possibility.
It is for the purpose of removing that deficiency as far as possible in respect of the section that my colleague the hon. member for Port Arthur has moved the amendment. Our group has given this section particular study. I think I can say that no clause of any bill which has been introduced into the house this session has received more consideration from this very small but very intelligent and very industrious group. We introduced this amendment because we believe it will achieve the common objective this group has in seeking to deal with the actions of this vermin of free enterprise which seeks to make a profit regardless of the welfare of our young people in Canada, and at the same time we are endeavouring to protect the rights of the free press and the right of free speech. Therefore I urge the minister to give serious consideration to our amendment in an effort to meet the needs of our times in those two directions.

Mr. Chairman, may I first say a word about one part of the amendment; the other part we will have a chance to study. I am directing my remarks to the

Criminal Code
part which proposes that for the words "a dominant characteristic" should be substituted "the dominant characteristic", which seems to us to make sense. However, if the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment would look at the French version of the bill, and if the minister would look at it, he would find that the French version of the bill meets that particular point, because the French version reads "la caracteristique dominante", whereas the English version is "a dominant characteristic". So far as the clause itself is concerned, I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken that all members of this house undoubtedly support the purpose of this amendment, and we hope that purpose will be achieved by the amendment. We hope those who have been sceptical about the result of this amendment, in that it will make additional work for lawyers-or as one person, Mr. Harold Weir in the June 23 issue, of the Vancouver Sun put it, that the only thing accomplished by this so-called definition is to make the problem of pinpointing obscenity more complex-will be proven wrong by this amendment if it becomes law.
What it does, of course, is tighten up legal sanctions against what we all recognize to be wrong and evil, obscenity; but these legal sanctions, even though they are tightened by this clause, will not have the effect we would like them to have if they do not have behind them perhaps the even more important moral sanction of public opinion. Bishop Gower said, as reported in the Vancouver Sun the other day:
It is society that is making this problem, and only society can cure it. If the change in law is a reflection of the desire of society as a whole, then it will be a change for the better.
We also hope, Mr. Chairman, that this tightening up can be brought about without interference-I know the minister hopes this also-with our traditional freedoms, our freedom of expression, which we cherish and which we do not want to see weakened. I am sure that by leaving this matter as it is intended in the hands of the courts we will get the kind of protection for our freedoms that we have the right to expect.
There is one aspect of this amendment with which perhaps the minister has dealt. If he has I apologize, but it has to do with the definition of "publication". When the problem was being discussed in the British House of Commons in the spring, the minister will perhaps remember that the solicitor general emphasized that while most discussion about obscenity had centred on authors

and books, the responsibility of the government was much wider than that and had to include things like records, pictures, films and television film tapes. Perhaps he could deal with that point.
I would like to say in conclusion that we heartily approve of the purpose of this amendment, and we hope this purpose will be achieved without interference with those freedoms which are of such great importance and which are always under threat these days.
As far as the other part of the amendment is concerned, that which would insert the words "and which is without literary or scientific merit", we would like to study it. I have the feeling that it is already covered, but we would like to look at it and express our views on that after the luncheon recess.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize it is just before one o'clock, but there is one point I would like to deal with now. I shall attempt after one o'clock to deal with every point which has been raised, but I want to deal with one point now to clear up a misapprehension.
The hon. member for Port Arthur said that in clause 12 we are shifting the onus of proof from the crown to the accused. I would like to correct that misapprehension at once and say that is not the case. If my hon. friend will read subsection 1 of the proposed section 150A, as he has done, he will see that the judge has first to be satisfied by information upon oath that there are reasonable grounds for believing that any publication is obscene. Then if he reads subsection 4, he will see it reads:
If the court is satisfied that the publication is obscene or a crime comic, it shall make an order declaring the matter forfeited to Her Majesty-
In each case, but particularly in subsection 4, which is the main consideration which has to be met before the order can be made, the court has to be satisfied. Mr. Chairman, the onus of satisfying the court is always on the crown; therefore it is perfectly clear that the crown has to discharge that onus of proof that the matter complained of is obscene within the new definition or the definition of the Hicklin case, whichever definition the crown wishes to rely upon.
I would like to dispose at once of any suggestion that we have put upon the man in whose possession the publication is found the onus of coming to court and proving that the publication is not obscene. He does not have to prove that. He has to come into

court to answer an allegation, yes. The allegation is that the matter is obscene, but there is no onus on him to prove it is not. The onus is still on the crown to prove that it is obscene before the court can be satisfied that it should make the order referred to.
In that connection I think my hon. friend was not quite clear in his reference by way of illustration to something which was proposed to be done in another bill, namely the bill to amend the combines act. My hon. friend said that we had again shifted the onus to the accused, and my hon. friend has missed the point. We have done nothing of the sort. What we have done is to create certain defences. We have made it clear that there are defences to a charge, and those defences were not established before. It is one thing to establish a defence, in which case of course the accused has to prove the defence; but that does not shift the burden of proof with respect to the charge itself to the accused. The crown still has to prove its charge. Then if the accused relies on certain defences, he has to prove them. All we have done there is to say that there are certain defences available, and then the accused has to prove them if he relies on them. Therefore in neither case have we placed any onus on the accused of proving his innocence; the onus is still on the crown to prove the offence as charged.

We did consider that point, which was what I undertook to do, but we came to the conclusion that because the question of proceeding against printers or publishers or anyone else who may be involved in this offence is primarily one for the law enforcement officers of the crown, and as the law enforcement officers of the Criminal Code are the attorneys general and other officials of the provincial governments, it did not seem very appropriate for the federal government to provide that there should be a prosecution of a printer or publisher in every case, or in any particular case. Of course a printer or publisher, if he is subject to the jurisdiction of our courts, can be proceeded against on the decision of the provincial attorney general or other prosecuting officer.
I would also remind the committee that inasmuch as we are providing this new procedure in rem we feel that this provides a quick, and as I have said before, objective method of disposing of the issue as to whether or not a publication is obscene, and it would be our expectation that, if the courts did decide that a certain publication was obscene, the matter would be finally disposed of and the publication withdrawn from circulation. Of course should a decision to this effect be given by the courts and the publisher or printer, or anyone else, persist in continuing the offence of publication in Canada, that person, whoever he might be, would be liable to prosecution with the consent of the attorney general.
In any part of Canada?
