That may be, Mr. Chairman; but I believe, for reasons I will explain, that the C.C.F. amendment is itself in error in seeking to incorporate the word mentioned therein. I shall deal with those reasons in a moment. "A" is the word we intended, as it appears in the English copy of the bill. If, therefore, the committee agrees with me and rejects the amendment of the C.C.F., I will move that the French version be corrected by deleting the word "la" where it appears and substituting therefor the word "une" which will make the English and French versions the same.
The reasons I suggested that the amendment moved by my friend the hon. member for Port Arthur should not be accepted are the following. We are trying to keep this bill as simple as possible and make it as simple as possible for the courts to find whether or not a publication is obscene. What is it that the courts are called upon to consider in making this finding? They will be called upon to consider whether it is a dominant characteristic of a publication that it unduly exploits sex, or sex and any one or more of several subjects, and it seems to me it is a simple question to put before the courts, to determine whether it is a dominant characteristic of a publication that might be in question.
If, however, you use the word "the"-it is "the" dominant characteristic of the publication in question-that does open all sorts of loopholes for legal argument of exactly the type which my hon. friends have previously criticized; because then you might have the lawyer for the defence suggesting that perhaps the dominant characteristic of the book is not this undue exploitation of sex, etc., but it is perhaps the artistic format of the book itself or some other characteristic of the book. If the courts answer the question that it is a dominant characteristic of a publication that it unduly exploits sex, I do not think the courts should be asked to make refinements as between other principal characteristics of the book and as to which one is the dominant and only characteristic. It is quite possible for a book to have more than one major characteristic.
If my hon. friends will look up the definition of "dominant" in the Oxford English dictionary they will find that one of the definitions-and I say it is one and not the only definition-is "occupying a commanding position". As an example of the use of the word "dominant" in that sense I give the following: "To take possession of the dominant parts of the globe", which indicates clearly

Criminal Code
that there may be a number of dominant parts or characteristics of a single whole. Therefore we have purposely used the words "a dominant characteristic" rather than "the dominant characteristic" for the reasons I have tried to indicate.
The other part of the proposed amendment would add the words "and which is without literary or scientific merit" so that the proposed clause would then read:
For the purposes of this act, any publication the dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex, or of sex and any one or more of the following subjects, namely, crime, horror, cruelty and violence and which is without literary or scientific merit, shall be deemed to be obscene.
I am sorry I cannot accept that part of the amendment either, for this reason. It seems to me that the insertion of those particular words would impose definitely upon a person who intended to publish an obscene book the necessity merely to put in one chapter, or indeed one paragraph, with literary or scientific merit, and then he would argue that this book did contain some passages of literary or scientific merit. Therefore, he would say, this book should not be found to be obscene.
We have provided in this section as it is drawn, Mr. Chairman, what we believe to be a fair, simple and conclusive test; namely, is a dominant characteristic of this book, or of other work, the undue exploitation of sex, or sex and crime or any one of a number of additional subjects? I think this is a simple question for a court to answer, and if the court can answer the question affirmatively, then I see nothing unfair in its bringing in a finding that the particular publication is obscene.
We do not want to open loopholes which, first, will permit of a number of unduly technical arguments; and, second, may well provide a loophole for escape on the part of those who should not really escape at all. Therefore I must say we cannot accept the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I was not very convinced by the definition of "dominant" the minister read out. I still think there can be really only one dominant characteristic of something. I believe the minister could or should elaborate even more on some examples of what are a series of dominant characteristics. I know in the field of heredity study the phrase, "genes with dominant characteristics" is used in the plural, but that is about the only field I can think of in which it is the practice.
To say that the amendment respecting literary and scientific merit might open the door to someone sneaking in something, I understood the minister to say the very reason

the words "undue exploitation" were used was to give protection to works of scientific, literary and artistic merit. If that is so, and since there may be a great deal of argument over "undue", I thought the addition of the direct phrase "and which is without literary and scientific merit" would correct that situation.
The minister emphasized throughout his remarks that this is a simple and objective way of getting at the problem that is presented to us. I wonder whether we really want it that simple. I wonder whether we really do not want the protection that we would get from having "the" instead of "a", and requiring that literary or scientific merit be considered. What is the magistrate going to do when this material is brought before him if it is not to make a decision as to whether the work has literary or scientific merit?
This brings me to the point where the minister said I was wrong in suggesting that the onus was being shifted from the crown to the defendant. Perhaps my choice of words was not fortunate; perhaps I did not make the point very well, but it certainly seems to me that this is a new procedure which is being tried by this amendment. For example, if a crusading police officer in a metropolitan city wanted to build up his reputation he could go around and make a number of seizures; or a crusading politician, as far as that is concerned, could go in and note some material and then take it to the magistrate or to the crown attorney and swear under oath that there were reasonable grounds for believing that this material was obscene. The material is all pulled off the shelves and the seller finds himself in court.
In effect, it seems to me that under subclause 3 he has to come in and show cause why the material should not be destroyed. What happens to him in the interval? It seems to me that by those seizures the court is putting him in a very serious situation. It could wind up by his getting into business difficulty, especially if his whole stock or a large portion of it was seized. It could certainly, because of the action of bringing him before the courts, bring him into disrepute and therefore put his business in difficulty. From that point of view I think this new procedure does put the defendant in an unusual position.
I wish I had more legal background so I could make a point about subclause 3 in effect forcing the defendant to show cause why the material should not be destroyed. I feel that this is something new, and I should like the minister to give us the precedents for this kind of procedure in law or in Canadian practice.

The other point I am not very satisfied with is this. Of course the minister assumes that the customs department, once they know a magistrate has ruled on a book, would not allow it into the country. If that is the way it is going to be, we could get all kinds of silly situations. I know the minister will remember the Senate committee that looked into the question of salacious and indecent literature in 1952 and 1953. I can well remember one of the most vicious blasts that were made in that committee was against a play by a British Columbia writer by the name of Ethel Wilson. Certainly a number of people in one of the provinces of Canada thought it was a most indecent and obscene thing and that the C.B.C. should never have been allowed to produce it; it was a foul and filthy thing. Well, by this sort of procedure, if Ethel Wilson had this book published in the United States we could wind up having some magistrate in one province decide that the book was obscene and the rest of Canada, where -it might be found quite acceptable, would be barred from reading it.
In the light of the fact that the Minister of National Revenue was very strong in his statement last year about wanting to get this question of making decisions on obscenity out of his department, I wonder whether the minister thinks this is a really satisfactory solution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the answer to the last question should be given at once and that is, yes; we do think it is a satisfactory solution because we are leaving the decision to the courts. The decision as to whether or not a publication is obscene is now to be made by the courts under this clause.
In answer to the other part of the hon. gentleman's remarks, I can only refer him again to the fact that the proposed subsections 1 and 4 should be read together. I emphasize that since subsection 4 says that if the court is satisfied that the publication is obscene it shall make an order declaring the matter forfeited to Her Majesty, this makes it clear that the crown has to satisfy the court.
Consider the situation that would exist if, for instance, neither side gave any evidence at all. Then the court would not be satisfied that the publication was obscene and the accused would be, I expect, acquitted. Let us put the other case-I am trying to illustrate the point to assure my hon. friend that there is no shifting of the onus-where the crown simply gave no evidence; then of course there would be nothing before the court upon which it could be satisfied. I think, therefore, we have clearly preserved the ordinary principle of law that it is the onus of the crown to
Criminal Code
prove its case. The case the crown is seeking to make clear, and which it has to prove, is that the publication complained of is obscene.
In so far as the "show cause" summons is concerned, I am quite frank to admit that it is a new procedure under circumstances of this kind. I could give one or two other examples, although I do not say they are parallel. I think particularly of a judgment summons which in effect calls upon the judgment debtor to show cause why he does not pay the judgment. If he fails to show cause he is liable to be put in prison, not for debt but for refusing to comply with a judgment of the court. The judgment debtor is therefore called into court to show cause why, in effect, he should not be committed for contempt of court by refusing to pay the judgment. There are other cases, but I cannot think of them at the moment, and I do not want to be inaccurate. The show cause summons is not a new thing. It is a new procedure with respect to obscenity, but it has been in force in the United Kingdom for over 100 years.
I should like also to deal with one other point made by my hon. friend, and that is the possibility of somebody in one province of Canada making a finding which my hon. friend alleges would be binding in all other parts of Canada, where perhaps the feeling was not the same. I can only emphasize again that there is, first of all, the right of appeal available to a person who feels himself aggrieved or who feels that somebody has not arrived at a proper decision. Second, not only the owner of the article seized but, under our proposal, the author is given the right to appear and make his representations refuting the crown's claim that the publication complained of is obscene.
Is it not true that in so falas the censorship of films is concerned, that is done directly within provincial compartments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, but there is no censorship here. This is one of the things I should perhaps emphasize at this point. We have set our faces against censorship so far as publications are concerned in the dominion parliament and we are seeking, under the ordinary legal principles applicable in Canada, to provide a method of dealing with publications which are offensive. I personally, as Minister of Justice have said-perhaps not as minister but certainly when I was a member of the opposition-that I could visualize no circumstances under which I would countenance the establishment of a bureau of censorship, certainly not in peacetime. It is because I recognize that there is a problem here, and it is because I am not prepared

Criminal Code
to recommend censorship, which I doubt would be acceptable to parliament, that we have sought this way of meeting the problem and still keeping within the confines of long accepted, well understood and sound principles of the Criminal Code, namely that a man is innocent until he is proven guilty. Here the publication is not obscene until it is proven to be obscene. What we are trying to do is define what we mean by obscene.

Speaking to the amendment I say, with all respect, that I do not share the view of the minister when he prefers the use of the term "a dominant feature", instead of "the dominant feature". My understanding is that there can be only one dominant feature, but I understand what the minister is trying to do. He is trying to bring under the section a case in which a feature may be an undue exploitation of sex but which does not necessarily constitute the dominant feature of that work. Perhaps the minister would consider eliminating the word "dominant" and using this language: "For the purpose of this act any publication, a feature of which is the undue exploitation of sex-". There you do not have to show that it is the dominant feature. So long as that work has in it a characteristic or a feature which is the undue exploitation of sex, then this wording might cover the situation, without making it necessarily the dominant feature.
I am just addressing myself to this one point. I should like to say something with regard to subsection 3 when we get to that.

The amendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur, Mr. Chairman, contains two points. First to substitute the word "the" for the word "a" after the words "any publication". As the Leader of the Opposition said this morning, the French translation of this section reads as follows:
( Translation):
-any publication a dominant characteristic of which is-
(Text):
Notwithstanding the arguments brought before the committee by the Minister of Justice I still believe that in this case, the French version should be adopted, substituting in the English text the word "the" for the word "a". There cannot be, in my opinion, more than one dominant characteristic. If the word "a" remains in this proposed new section it will then mean that a publication could have more than one dominant characteristic, which is difficult to conceive. I admit that a publication can be marked by many characteristics, but if one of those is the dominant one it should be termed "the" dominant and not "a" dominant characteristic, otherwise the word "dominant" would lose its meaning.

As to the second part of the amendment, that is the insertion following the word "violence" of the words, "and which is without literary or artistic merit", I simply say that part of the amendment adds nothing to the clarification of the definition of obscenity suggested by the Minister of Justice. The words in the new definition contained in this bill, "dominant characteristic", would in my opinion take care of a production which is a literary or scientific work. Even if isolated passages of such a publication would exploit sex and other immoral subjects, if the dominant characteristic of that publication is of real value in literature or science this new suggested definition of obscenity would not apply.
The proposed amendment to the section under study-I refer to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur -would perhaps complicate the task of the judge who would then have to decide on the literary or scientific merit of the publication suspected of obscenity. More evidence would then be needed to enlighten the judge and to help him to decide upon the literary or scientific merit of the production under examination.
Evidence of fact has always been admitted before our courts, and exceptionally evidence of opinion is generally admissible whenever an issue comprises a subject in which knowledge can only be secured from experts or scientists. This amendment, I believe, in order to meet the requirements of all our acts, should also contain something along this line; that the opinion of experts as to the literary and scientific merit of an article may be admitted in any proceedings under this act. The amendment, if accepted, should also be moved under section 12 of this bill adding paragraph 150A to the Criminal Code; and to be complete it should also include the words "art or learning or of other objects of general concern".

Mr. Chairman, there is no perfect system of law, but I think we can take it that we have achieved the least imperfect jurisprudence because we have been wise enough to realize that it is difficult if not impossible to chart in advance in its entirety or to define with accuracy and precision all the countless relationships between individuals or between individuals and the state. We have been content, and I think properly so, to leave to our courts and to men who are learned in the law, dedicated to their calling and very knowledgeable in the facts of human nature, sufficient room in which to manoeuvre to draw the distinctions and make the refinements necessary to arrive at the greatest measure of justice.

Show me any system or any code of conduct of human beings where an attempt is made to cover every contingency, to cabin, crib and confine within narrow limits behind high walls all the various matters which may be considered by a court, and there you will see a greater volume of litigation and a greater amount of jurisprudence than in any other system of law of which I know. I think, for example, of the revenue laws and the liquor laws of the respective provinces.
But having said that, I still think here is a case where amendment has long been needed to bring this particular aspect of the criminal law into line with the present-day situation. As the minister said, one of the leading cases on this particular branch of the criminal law is one which was decided in the United Kingdom shortly after the middle of the last century. I have before me the latest annotated Criminal Code and the cases referred to under section 150. The latest criminal case in Canada was Rex v. Ballan-tyne, decided in 1916. Both these cases were obviously decided at a time when there was not considered nor was there even contemplated all the volume of filthy and salacious literature which has descended upon us in recent years. For that reason it is quite obvious that we have needed for some time an amendment which will act as a beacon and a guide to courts in dealing with this particularly knotty problem.
Dealing very briefly with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur, may I say this. 1 am quite satisfied that if this amendment which he seeks was in fact enacted it would greatly increase the amount of litigation and the number of contested cases. Counsel for the defence would have a field day with an opportunity to make use of an amendment of that kind. As I think the hon. member who just took his seat said, what is of literary or scientific merit? As the minister himself said, any small portion of a publication could be directed to a high level of literary or scientific merit, and there would be a perfect defence. I suggest that the adoption of this amendment would certainly not achieve the results which the hon. member may be trying to seek.
Before I take my seat there is one matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister pertaining to section 12 of the bill or section 150 of the Code. It seems to me to give a simple and expeditious method by which the crown could inquire whether or not a publication is obscene having in mind the fact that the definition in section 150 lists the variety of people who may be the subject of a criminal charge:
Criminal Code
(1) Everyone commits an offence who
(a) makes, prints, publishes, distributes, circulates, or has in his possession-
I am wondering whether it would not be possible for any one of the people falling within those categories to be able himself to come before a court and say, "I have in my possession certain publications and I am doubtful whether or not they are obscene within the definition which has been enacted" and thereby simply and cheaply ask the court for a declaration as to that particular matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that could be very
simply accomplished, in the proposal before us, in that all that person would have to do would be to get somebody else, his lawyer or someone, to lay an information with respect to the particular matter about which he was concerned. In that way he could very quickly get before the courts.

Earlier in the session
I had prepared notes for a speech I had intended to make on this subject. However, at this stage of the session such a speech, as detailed and exhaustive as I intended it to be, would be quite inappropriate. Consequently I should like to confine my comments to half a dozen sentences.
First I wish to state that I believe the present proposal constitutes a constructive and forward-looking attempt to deal with a problem which is as difficult as it has become alarming. The steep increase in the sale of salacious and depraved periodicals, of corrupt and rotten publications is a threat to our established national standards of conduct and decency.
In large measure this increase is the result of the illicit, clandestine activities of certain distributors to compel retailers to handle these offensive magazines as a condition precedent to receiving for sale other periodicals. Especially, Mr. Chairman, do I hope that section 150B will be rigidly enforced in order to eliminate these purveyors of putridity, these profiteers in pornography.
In my view the amendment that has been presented to the committee by the hon. member for Port Arthur would render that section totally unworkable and would pull any teeth which it has. For that reason I intend to vote against it.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to add a few comments which I feel may assist the Minister of Justice in bringing before this committee the amendment he has in mind, because I find this is possibly one of the most important pieces of legislation which we have faced for some weeks. I realize that in these troubled times if the moral standards of our community are to be upheld,

Criminal Code
this may be the means of achieving a victory which could not be achieved in other ways.
Comments were made to the effect that this is a matter into which politics could not enter. 1 regret very much the remarks of the Minister of Justice last Wednesday when this matter first came up and when he indicated his opinion as to the remarks made by hon. members of the opposition. I was further surprised this morning when the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm stated that this amendment presented to the house was a total remedy for the evil presently existing. I am speaking on this matter because I feel it is most important.
In our area a short time ago it was alleged that two children of 10 or 11 years of age burned a $1 million school, their own school, after having inscribed on some of the blackboards a remark indicating their intentions. When such things occur there is no doubt that these young people, knowing the act they were about to commit, were prompted by their imaginations, which possibly had been led astray by crime comics or other literature which unfortunately had been furnished to them.
I must state at this stage that I feel the Minister of Justice has failed to include in this amendment a higher penalty if the sale is made to a minor instead of to an adult. I am sure that if we are to protect the Canadian people under the new law of this country, we must certainly protect the minors. We have provisions in many statutes in our country, both provincial and federal, whereby a crime, especially a crime against morals, carries a greater penalty when it is committed against an infant. I am sure it will be a surprise to the Canadian people when they see that an amendment such as this does not include that provision in what has been stated by some hon. members to be a total remedy to the evil.
We are trying to bring about in our Criminal Code of Canada a definition of what we consider a crime so that the judges of this country, in each of the provinces, will decide what is the evil we are trying to prevent. We cannot assume in this regard that we are both the legislative and administrative body in this country. It is very wrong for this parliament to bring in a piece of legislation feeling that judges will necessarily take the opinions or interpretations which we have today placed upon them; therefore it is our duty to be accurate when we define this crime which we are trying to prevent. I would like to quote on that score a paragraph from a very fine article which appeared in August, 1958 in

the periodical or review Relations. There is an editorial on page 197 to this effect: (Translation):
In order to be effective, the law must conform to the exacting standards of natural ethics, and define them so clearly that no amount of pettifoggery can distort their meaning or impair their scope.
(Text):
Mr. Chairman, this definition which is now being placed in our Code fails in many aspects in trying properly to define the crime for which our judges will punish the guilty ones. It will open doors which will necessarily permit the defence lawyers to discuss at greater length the merits of the offence. Therefore I would like, in assisting this committee, to make some comments of my own concerning the possible interpretations which could come about.
The first is one which the Minister of Justice just a moment ago pretended to solve in replying to the Leader of the Opposition, when he used the word "publication" in the clause relating to obscenity. Many things are defined by the Code as obscene; and, of course, a person found having such a publication or other matter in his possession for the purpose of sale, and so on, is guilty of an offence. Now, however, the definition simply says a "publication". I think when the Minister of Justice starts to think how you can define a dominant characteristic, or an undue exploitation of sex, in anything but a publication, I am sure the judges would also want to consider, for example, a photograph or a phonograph record.
The Minister of Justice says he is bringing forward this amendment for the purpose of clarifying the position, but he is not clarifying the position as far as, for example, models or pictures, or articles such as a deck of cards are concerned. I feel that a judge, when adjudicating upon this matter and having the word "publication" before him in the statute, will be unable to find that such an article as a deck of cards can be described as a publication. Therefore I think the words should be repeated as we find them in the old section so that all these matters are covered. This will have some relevancy to these other matters considered under clause 12, such as a tied sale. For example, you could have a tied sale of an article, or a tied sale of a film, as well as a publication. And such is in no way covered by this statute.
We have also heard some discussion about the word "dominant" and the words "the" and "a". I feel that the trouble has occurred because of the use of the word "dominant". I think the intention of the Minister of Justice is to define it as meaning a great part or an important part; but the word "dominant" means a majority. To most of the people in

this house it means over 50 per cent. What will it mean to the courts? Possibly the same thing.
I can also see certain publications, especially in the domain of magazines, where you may have ten articles, no two of which the subject matter are connected. I realize that the hon. member for Port Arthur, who is a librarian, is thinking of books of say 600 pages, containing a few pages which may be found objectionable; therefore the book should not be condemned because of that. But when you are dealing with magazines and publications you may find 15 articles in the magazine, two of which are most objectionable, the other 13 not being objectionable. In that case you might have two very bad pieces of obscene literature; how can you fit in the word "dominant" if the word "dominant" means the majority, over 50 per cent, and so on? I think the intention is to condemn books or magazines wherein you find an important, undue exploitation of sex.
In trying to find the meaning behind the use of the word "a" or "the", as I stated, you can have a magazine containing eight articles all unrelated, six of which pertain to sports and the remaining two to something absolutely immoral. Now, by the meaning of the word "dominant" could you find a magazine obscene for six articles out of eight, the six sports and two only concerning obscene literature?
I would like to say something about section 150A. The minister has a new procedure, and intended well, but what exactly does it do? You have subsection 4 whereby you cannot seize an article or a model or a photographic record and find it obscene. I think that the same words should be used to start the clause as in the original section 150 to ascertain that you could have these articles found obscene and forfeited to the crown in the right of the province in the same way, but I fail to see that a publication would mean an article or an instrument as subsection 4 states.
There is something that can be said about the assignment of the onus-why it says in subclause 2 that the person against whom the complaint is made may appear before a court and show cause why the matter seized should not be forfeited. Other words could be used. He could appear on his own defence, but if he does not appear to show cause why it should not be forfeited many magistrates may take it for granted that if someone does not show cause, automatically, without reading the book or getting the required evidence, it is obscene. I realize what is said in clause 4, but magistrates may consider themselves satisfied because they did not
Criminal Code
find someone to show cause and they would have the accused admitting the crime in a sense and therefore I feel that it is not the intention of parliament to shift the onus, and the words "show cause" could be replaced by "defence".
Then we have the fact which I think most important that if a motion is made for an order under this amendment no other proceedings in the province can be had under section 150 without the consent of the attorney general. This is giving the administration of our criminal law to elected representatives. There could be a situation in which there were only five books out of a publication of 10,000 in a province and people might make it a point to appear before the magistrate and lay a charge against their own people so that they might pay a fine on five books and the whole matter is stopped and cases which have begun under section 150 must be discontinued, cases, say, where 500 or 1,000 books have been seized or where a charge has been laid under section 150. These charges will be discontinued unless an elected representative, the attorney general of the province, will grant permission, and I fail to realize why the criminal law should be placed in this manner in the hands of an elected person. That is certainly a fault which can be found readily.
Further, why could it not be if five books are found obscene within a province that all the copies of that obscene literature would thereby be condemned and could be forfeited to the crown? It seems to me that that would be a very small step and that would take off our shelves in each of the provinces those books which are thought obscene by a judge of the province, because the way this clause is made even on an order made when the judge is not satisfied that the material is obscene, that can occur, and if an order is made by a magistrate in one part of a province that that literature is not obscene, it will thereby bar all other cases in the province unless the attorney general can review the matter and say possibly that this first magistrate was wrong and permit a trial under section 150.
I feel that possibly the amendment suggested may not be the most correct one, but I am fully aware that the amendment does not satisfy the need of this country to condemn false scientific works. A lot of books on the shelves today are being sold for no other reason than to arouse interest in obscene literature and so on and there is absolutely nothing brought forward to take care of that difficulty where people will hide behind the fact that it is an effort to put out a scientific book. I fully realize that to bring about a proper solution of this evil in this

Criminal Code
country no doubt the co-operation of the people is required and I apprehend that many Canadian organizations realize that; but notwithstanding the fact that if an amendment of this kind is to be brought in it should do away with all these possibilities that laymen like ourselves could not take on ourselves. There is always the possibility that the judges will interpret these terms in a way different from the way in which we interpret them today; they will go to technical terminology and to the dictionary and I doubt that they will as above stated condemn an article or a film under the word "publication". Undoubtedly the minister is trying to do a good thing, but I feel that though he has had objectives which were stated to be political, he is being in this instance absolutely conservative. We have heard that a conservative is sometimes a person who acts hastily after thinking over a thing too long. The minister has thought about this a lot and in the dying days of this session he brings in an amendment which many institutions in this country had no time to study and report to their representative.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not think the committee need apologize for having spent a certain amount of time on this clause, since it is as complicated as it is important; important not only in relation to social health and public morality but also in its implications concerning at least one of our traditional freedoms. The minister has emphasized both in this house and outside that he has no desire to introduce anything in the nature of censorship. I am sure he is quite sincere in that, and I am not suggesting that this particular clause does that, but it is something about which we want to be as certain in our own minds as we can be. The hon. member for Peace River when he intervened a few moments ago expressed some anxiety about the amendment to the amendment which is before us in that it might encourage litigation and makes things more complicated. When things are complicated lawyers usually have a better opportunity of intervening. I can say that, not being a lawyer. The difficulty and perhaps, in a sense, even the danger of this kind of legislation in general dealing with this subject is that in the words of, perhaps it was Dicey, though I admit it was in a different context, it tends to substitute litigation for legislation. That is one of the things which has worried a number of members about this kind of amendment.
In so far as the amendment of the hon. member for Port Arthur is concerned I felt that the original French text was more logical than the present English text, but which, as the minister pointed out, is the official text.

When you talk about something being dominant you think of something being almost exclusive; a characteristic which is dominant does surely, at least in my understanding of it, exclude other and secondary characteristics in respect of any particular matter. Perhaps the minister will be able to explain to our satisfaction how in a publication there could be four, five or six characteristics each of which is dominant. The very concept of dominancy means it is superior to other concepts. That is why it seems to me that the amendment of the hon. member for Port Arthur is a logical and reasonable one. The other part of the amendment seems to me to be a little more difficult to support.
I would ask the minister this question. If a particular publication does have literary or scientific merit, can its dominant characteristic then be the undue exploitation of sex? If the answer to that is no, then perhaps the amendment is redundant. I noticed that the British parliament-and no doubt the minister has also noticed it-in discussing this subject last February did include a clause in the bill they were considering to deal with the particular problem which was raised in this committee by the hon. member for Port Arthur. The clause introduced in England reads:
A person shall not be convicted of an offence against this section if he proves that his publication of the matter in question is justified as being for the public good on the ground that it furthers the interest of science, literature, art or learning, or of other objects of general concern.
I think I am right in saying that this particular clause was included in the British bill and passed after a great deal of discussion and some amendment. If I am wrong, the minister will correct me on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I ask the Leader of the Opposition if the bill to which he is referring is the obscene publications bill of this year?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am referring to the one introduced last February, or at any rate last spring. I am reading from a passage in an article published in the London Times of February 27, 1959, referring to that bill. The British parliament after a long discussion, much longer than we are having, which included committee discussion, felt it was desirable and indeed necessary to include that paragraph. Does the minister think that point is sufficiently met in the amendment he has himself introduced at this time? I again ask him the question which it seems to me has a bearing on this. If any publication is of literary or scientific merit, can its dominant characteristic be the undue exploitation of sex?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that it is difficult to be dogmatic and completely certain about the word "dominant" and whether it should be "a" dominant characteristic or "the" dominant characteristic. Perhaps I can try to illustrate the point of view which I believe the courts will take and which my officials after long and careful consideration have felt argues in favour of the use of the word "a" instead of "the". There are those hon. gentlemen opposite who ask, "How can a book have more than one dominant characteristic," and who say if their argument is correct the word should be ''the" and not "a".
Let us say that you have a valley adjacent to which are three mountain peaks of equal height. Which of those peaks is the dominant peak? Or let us take another illustration. Let us assume you have a book-and it is dangerous to attempt to be too particular in these matters-which purports to be a study of sociological problems and in that book the author has gone about treating the subject in a manner which involves the use of illustrations of sexual relations arising in the course of the thing, as a secondary characteristic, which leads the law officers and, let us say, which we think would lead a court to assume that it is an obscene publication. It might be argued that there are two dominant characteristics of this book. In the first place it is a book dealing with sociological problems and consequently an undue exploitation of sex, and containing illustrations or scenes of sex or illicit relations. In this sense I think it is possible for there to be so many characteristics of a book or publication-let us not confine it to books-which are not necessarily of a related nature that it would be impossible, and thus defeat the purpose of the clause, if you required the court in each case to say that the only dominant characteristic of the book-in the sense of there being only one dominant characteristic-is that it unduly exploits sex or sex and one or more of the other subjects named.
I believe there are cases in which it is a profitless task to seek to isolate a thing as being the only dominant characteristic and it is for that reason we have purposely used the words "a dominant characteristic". I ask hon. members to consider the over-all effect of the question which the court is going to be called upon to decide before there is a conviction. That is to say, the court will have to decide that this is a publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex or of sex and any one or more of the subjects named. I do not think the use of the words "a dominant characteristic" in that over-all context poses the court
Criminal Code
with any obstacle which it cannot answer for itself or which makes it necessary for the court to be asked to answer the question as to whether or not this is the only dominant characteristic of the publication.

Would the minister permit a question, Mr. Chairman. Would it not be better to use the word "prominent"? The reference would then be to a prominent characteristic rather than a dominant characteristic.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are two reasons why we rejected words of that type. In the first place we did not want to spread the net so wide that we caught books, as it were, without any real possibility of successful defence and about which there is room for genuine controversy. There are so many books I can think of of which the prominent characteristic in certain passages is the exploitation of sex. We wanted to go no farther than that. The other reason is this. The main concern we have in mind and which we are framing this amendment in an attempt to meet is the pulp trash type of stuff that is appearing in such vast quantities on our newsstands. While I do not for a moment pretend to be unconcerned about the major book type of publication, I must say I am far less concerned about that type and less concerned if one or two such books escape, than I would be in allowing this other stuff, about which there is really no genuine controversy to escape because we over-refined the amendment we are trying to introduce.
The Leader of the Opposition raised a very good question about this matter of whether it should be a defence to show that the work contributed to the public good. I would refer him to section 150, subsection 3, of our present Criminal Code which contains a provision very similar to that contained in the British obscene publications bill to which he referred. The subsection reads:
(3) No person shall be convicted of an offence under this section-
Section 150, which creates the offence of obscenity. I continue:
-if he establishes that the public good was served by the acts that are alleged to constitute the offence and that the acts alleged did not extend beyond what served the public good.

Mr. Chairman, if the minister attaches so much importance to retaining the word "a" instead of the word "the" in the English version, why does he leave the word "la" instead of "une" in the French version?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have already explained that if the committee agrees with me in rejecting the amendment now before

Criminal Code
us, I will then move that the word "la" be changed to "une", in the French version.

Will the minister please
explain how the clause would be affected it he left out the word "dominant" altogether and simply said "a characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of", or a feature of it "is the undue exploitation of"; leave the word "dominant" out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Again I say, Mr. Chairman, if we did that then we would cast a net to catch a number of things that we really do not want to catch under this definition at all. We designed this definition having in mind the type of pulp trash that appears on the newsstands. I said I am not unconcerned about the others but I am mostly concerned about dealing with that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has, I think, made a pretty reasonable explanation of the wording which he has put before the committee. May I ask him one further question? This is a matter, as I recall it, which received a good deal of consideration also at Westminster. I ask this question as a layman. Perhaps if I were a lawyer I would know more. Would there be any difficulty in the way of expert evidence being acceptable before a court which would have a bearing on the literary, scientific and other qualities of a particular publication?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I explained earlier that our attempt here is to produce an objective definition, or as objective as we can make it, to introduce a number of pretty factual tests by which the court is asked to measure this question of obscenity. It is my view that this type of definition does not lend itself to the giving of opinion evidence by experts. If, as was the case when the only definition we had was the Hicklin definition, your definition is almost entirely subjective, if it has to be interpreted in the light of what are its effects on certain individuals, then, I think, there is much more room for opinion evidence. But I point out to my friend that actually, even when we had only the Hicklin definition, the Ontario court of appeal in the American News case, in the judgment of Mr. Justice Laidlaw expressly ruled that opinion evidence was not admissible, on the grounds, in his opinion, that it was irrelevant.
I go back, having made these explanations as to our present thinking, to repeat what I said earlier, that we feel we are moving in this field. This approach is, I believe, objective but if you like I am prepared to regard it only as a preliminary move. I recognize that in the United Kingdom, they have given a great deal of consideration to

it and they put a provision in their bill allowing for expert evidence. We will watch the experience there and we will also carefully watch the experience here and we will be prepared to reconsider the matter in the light of the experience.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As far as I am concerned I merely wish to add that, with the minister's explanation, I am prepared to support the clause as it stands and I hope it will have the effect that we all desire.

Mr. Chairman, as was indicated by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), a member should not be reproached with slowing down the proceedings if he chooses to make a few remarks.
Upon receiving both versions, the French and the English, I looked through them carefully, and found that the English version said this:
(Text):
Any publication a dominant characteristic- (Translation):
Whereas in French, I found this:
-publication dont la caracteristique dominante-

One might then conclude that in the text or picture there may be more than one char-

acteristic which are precisely of the nature referred to in section 11.
Now, in the second place, I believe that amendment proposed by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) is unwarranted, first because of the reasons outlined by the Minister of Justice, and then, one must not forget that we are dealing with a matter covered by the Criminal Code and that the mens rea, criminal intent, must be established. If a scientist should be brought to court for utilizing or having in his possession one of those publications, we still have to prove that, having those publications in hand, he had some criminal intent; unless that is proven there can be no proof of the offence with which he is charged.
Furthermore, as the Minister of Justice said a moment ago, if the matter involves no danger for the public welfare, the common weal, the accused cannot be found guilty.
Now, in closing, I suggest it is extremely difficult to find a definition of obscenity. I listened to the article read into the record by the hon. member for Nickel-Belt (Mr. Godin) and I must say that even the authors of that article, the editors of that magazine, who tried to devise a definition, failed in the attempt.
In my opinion, the definition which is being proposed today will adequately serve the needs of the population, and the Minister of Justice-
You obviously have not read the definition.

I shall go on with my remarks, and I would ask the hon. member for Nickel-Belt to ask his question after, if he sees fit.
I say that, with experience, a way will be found to correct this definition. I think the main result of introducing this definition into the Criminal Code will be to make people who are in the habit of keeping such publications on their shelves more careful about checking to see whether the publications are obscene or not, and to make sure, before buying such publications or books, that they are not such as to sully the mind.
And if I may be allowed to express a wish, I hope that, when the definition is adopted, the C.B.C. will have proper regard for it in the production of their TV programs.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to remind the hon. member who has just spoken that he brought in the matter of mens rea. If he reads section 150 of the code as it now stands he will see that mens rea is not a matter for consideration in this crime. Subsection 6 of section 150 of the code reads:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then, Mr. Chairman, in pursuance of the explanation I made earlier I shall ask one of my colleagues to move that clause 11 of the French version of Bill C-58, be amended by deleting the word "la" where it appears at line 13 on page 4 of the said version and substituting therefor the word "une". I shall ask my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs to move that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I so move.
Would the minister explain what the significance of the amendment is?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The significance of the amendment is to bring the French version into line with the English version, in accordance with the vote of the committee which has just been taken.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
I should like the minister to explain how the courts are going to use the definition on matters other than publications?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry, but I did not catch the question.

The amendment by subsection 8 of section 150 seems to apply to publications only and I fail to see, in the absence of any explanation by the minister, how other matters which may be obscene, such as articles, could be covered by this definition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that will be done because section 150, subsection 1, of the Criminal Code reads as follows:
Everyone commits an offence who
(a) makes, prints, publishes, distributes, circulates, or has in his possession for the purpose of publication, distribution or circulation any obscene written matter, picture, model, phonograph record or other thing whatsoever,
Just by reference to the word "publication" in subsection 1 of section 150, I believe the use of the word "publication" in the new subsection 8 to be added to section 150, will extend the coverage of the section to include pictures or phonograph records, because it is obvious that what is contemplated now by section 150 is the publication of phonograph records. In the new subsection 8 we refer to publication, the dominant characteristic of which is. I think, therefore, it is most likely that the courts would

Criminal Code
understand this use of the word "publication" in connection with articles such as phonograph records.
I want to make it clear when I say that, that that is my opinion and the opinion of my legal advisers. Our primary intention, as I have made clear before, was to catch this type of trash that was appearing on the newsstands. This was our main intention and is the reason we did not add words to make it doubly certain that it would cover this other type of article which my hon. friend has in mind. If it appears on the basis of experience that we should extend this to cover such things as phonograph records, and if it appears particularly it is the desire of parliament to do so, I would be glad on another occasion to consider making it quite clear, especially if the courts do not agree with my interpretation that this includes other articles.
The minister's explanation may be true, but how would the minister explain the application in section 150A? How can you address section 150A to phonograph records?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The answer to that, I think, must be that in this section we did not have anything in mind other than written publications. I am not nearly as certain of that as I am about the earlier section, but in this section we were concerned with written publications appearing on the newsstands.
In so far as section 150A is concerned, it is not the intention of this government to make it applicable to these other obscene matters?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is our intention to make it expressly applicable to the written publications which are appearing on the newsstands. We did not intend to make it non-applicable to these others, but we did have written publications particularly in mind.
Will section 150B apply if the article is other than a written publication?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that is clearly confined to written publications because it uses the words, "copies of any other publication". I do not see how that could be anything other than a written publication.

Has the minister considered specifically exempting libraries from section 150A, where it says that a judge who is satisfied by information upon oath that there are reasonable grounds for believing that any publication, copies of which are kept for sale or distribution and so on; was there any consideration given to exempting libraries from this section because they are distributors? The reason I raise the matter is that it is quite conceivable you might get-I do

not want to use the word a "crackpot"- somebody who had a very narrow interest in this field, and he could make it very difficult for public libraries in relation to the books they might have on their shelves. I just wondered whether the minister had given any thought to these people?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not believe it would be wise to exempt libraries from this clause. After all, a complainant will have to go to a judge and satisfy the judge that the matter is obscene. I point out here, and perhaps I should have dealt with it earlier in reply to the hon. member for Nickel Belt, that the provisions of subsection 7 make it clear that there will be no prosecution in respect of a publication found to be obscene under this section without the consent of the attorney general. It was for the purpose of preventing victimizing persons who would, in a loose sense of the word, be regarded as distributors, that we provided this quick method of getting a decision on the merits of the issue and then the prosecution with respect to these items will only be launched with the consent of the attorney general.
If someone did have their own private collection, would it be perfectly legitimate under this section, no matter what sort of publication there was in it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the answer to that question is generally yes. I give that answer because of the wording of subclause 1 of the proposed section 150A wherein it is provided that a judge has to be satisfied.
-that there are reasonable grounds for believing that any publication, copies of which are kept for sale or distribution in premises within the jurisdiction of the court, is obscene-
Only then is an offence committed. That would not normally apply to a person who had a private collection in his house although I think one would have to read the recent case of the Queen against Berringer, a maritime case, in order to be absolutely certain of your ground there. That case is interesting when I read it-and I have just read it hurriedly-in that it discusses the case where a person with a private collection invited others in to view it, and whether than can be circulation or publication. If it is purely a private collection there would be no possibility of an adverse verdict under this section.

I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to subsection 6 which provides:
(6) An appeal lies from an order made under subsection (4) or (5) by any person who appeared in the proceedings-
Suppose an individual has brought this matter to the attention of the magistrate. Does

this mean that this individual and the crown attorney and the defendant, all three, would have the right of appeal or any one of the three?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only persons who would have the right of appeal are those who are represented in a technical sense in the proceedings. The attorney general or the crown prosecutor or the crown, shall I say, certainly if either appeared and was represented in the proceedings in defence, I think he would have the right of appeal. If the owner, that is to say the distributor or person on whose premises it was found appeared, he would have the right of appeal also.

Suppose in a small town there was a league of decency and they went out and picked up these books and brought them to the attention of the magistrate. They would have nothing to do with this matter at all. They would have no right of appearing in an appeal on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If this prosecution were initiated by such an organization or an individual as a private prosecutor to appear, then he or she would have the right of appeal. If, however, he merely laid an information and the crown carried the prosecution, the private individual would have no right of appeal.

The minister told us that this definition in this section or in these two sections are aimed practically at the pulp trash. I am sure we must agree with that objective. But the corruption comes from reading this stuff. Why do people read it? They read it because they are attracted to it on the newsstands by some lurid title or by some lurid picture on the cover. Is there anything anywhere else in the Criminal Code by which that sort of thing could be prohibited or by which we could destroy the attractiveness of this literature on the newsstands to people by way of the picture and the title.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I hope that we will have done it by the combination of section 150 of the code as it presently stands and the new amendments that we are now introducing. If in fact these publications are obscene-and I think the ones to which my hon. friend refers are obscene-and are so found under the new definition, then they will be subject to immediate removal from the newsstands because they are forfeit to the crown. I think the effective thing to do would be to provide a means, as we have tried to do here, of getting at the publication itself; because if we do that we have also incidentally got at the devices by which they are publicized and made attractive.
Criminal Code

What is the procedure when somebody has informed a judge or magistrate that a certain person has books on the shelf for sale as to which there are reasonable grounds for believing they are obscene and these books are confiscated and are found to be obscene by the judge and there is no appeal. What is the procedure for eliminating these books from all the other bookshelves throughout the country or in the same city.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would be up to the law enforcement officers of the crown. If those books were found upon any other book shelf or upon any other book store shelves for sale I would imagine that the sensible thing to do would be for the crown attorney or the police officers to inform the individuals concerned that they had better get them off their shelves, not because the police officer thinks so but because the court has found them to be obscene. If the person in question disregarded such a warning, then I imagine there would be a prosecution because then I should think that the attorney general would consent to a prosecution under clause 7 of the amendment we are now introducing. But while it is true that ignorance of the law is no excuse, we put that in on purpose so that there would be an opportunity of warning a person and if he voluntarily withdrew the books from circulation, then we would hope that the attorney general would not authorize a prosecution. But if he defied a verdict of the court and continued to offer them for sale, then I should think the attorney general would order a prosecution.
How would a news vendor or a bookstore in Newfoundland know that something like this had happened in Quebec, for example.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have just suggested that it would be up to the crown attorney or the police officers who have knowledge of these things to warn persons who are found selling them that there has been a decision of the court that they are obscene and that they had better get them off their shelves. After all, in this matter I should also say that we rely-and I am sure that all law enforcement officers must do so-upon the assistance of well-intentioned individuals, service clubs, religious organizations and others who will be, I am quite satisfied, very watchful of developments in this sphere. They will be watching to see what are the decisions of the courts in various parts of the country or, in particular, in their own province and they will bring to the attention of the responsible officials, if the responsible officials miss it, knowledge of such verdicts. Then, as I say they

Criminal Code
can warn the persons who may be continuing to sell these articles and give them a chance to withdraw them. The reason we put in clause 7 is, however, to permit of a warning being given and to provide that the attorney general must consent to a prosecution in the expectation that he would not consent to a prosecution unless a warning had been given but would authorize a prosecution when the warning was disregarded.

May I ask the minister whether he feels that if in one province an order has been made declaring certain literature or publication to be obscene it is required for the purpose of confiscation under clause 150A that these motions be repeated in all areas where these books are found for the purpose of confiscation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the usual situation. Each province is responsible for the enforcement of the law within its territorial areas.
The minister means that in every community concerning every store in the province a motion will have to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, not at all. I have endeavoured to explain the situation as I would see it develop. Let us for example take my own province. Suppose in the city of Vancouver there is a proceeding under new section 150A and the publication is adjudged to be obscene. The crown prosecutor of the city of Vancouver will know about it. His policemen, I would think, would be instructed to be on the lookout for that publication in any of the stores. If they see it they will warn the proprietor, I would think, that there has been a judgment and that this book has been found to be obscene.
I should think that would produce the result that within a reasonable time all those publications would be withdrawn in that city. I would also imagine the attorney general of the province would be aware of the decisions of the courts of the province and would instruct his departmental agents throughout the province and the police, who are the agents of the attorney general in this matter, and in that way word would be disseminated throughout the province. All you would need is to issue a warning, and if there was a refusal to comply you could prosecute under the new clause 150.
Clause as amended agreed to.
On clause 12-Warrant of seizure.

We were discussing clause 12, Mr. Chairman, only in relation to clause 11. I think we might deal with clause 12 much more directly, and I would like to concern myself with the first part of the clause. This clause creates what we know

in civil law as a seizure before judgment. In other words, the right is given, by information upon oath, to walk in and effect a seizure at once before guilt has been established. It is true there has been a complaint under oath, but I would compare it with a search warrant where there has been no conviction. Here we have a similar sort of right given, and it is a new concept, I think, in our criminal law; it is a form of invasion upon civil property.
Assuming then that a warrant is sworn out upon oath, seizure is effected and the judge comes to the conclusion, as the clause says further on, that it is not obscene and the merchandise should be returned, a very difficult situation would develop there. The business of this man might have been seriously affected, if not altogether ruined. It is true that the clause speaks of expeditious action to be taken within seven days. But the judge must make a decision, and assuming he comes to the decision that it is not salacious or obscene and therefore orders the merchandise to be returned, what right of action has a person whose business has been thus invaded merely because information was provided upon oath? Has he a right in damages against the person who has sworn the complaint? Will he have the right to proceed in damages against an officer of the crown who in good faith may have thought the publications were obscene and who was of the opinion that it was a fit subject to be confiscated?
Would the minister inform the committee, as I am sure he is able to do, how a victim of this treatment, for example a merchant who suffers an unjustified raid upon his store, as it subsequently, turns out to be in the opinion of the judge, has any remedy to be restored to the same position he was in before that unjustified raid was made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no remedy, Mr. Chairman. If the warrant was properly taken out, there is no remedy in damages against anybody. I would like to direct my hon. friend's attention to subclause 5, which provides that if the court is not satisfied that the publication is obscene it shall order it to be returned to the person from whom it was seized. There are also in addition a number of other cases where there is authority given in the Criminal Code for persons to enter and make seizures of articles before there has been proof of guilt. I refer my hon. friend, for example, to section 429 (1) where there is provision for authorizing the seizing of anything in a building, receptacle or place in respect of which there is reasonable ground to believe it will afford evidence with respect to the commission of an offence against the act. There are some other cases as well in which seizure

is authorized without proof of guilt and there is no right of action, to use my friend's words, given to the person from whom the property has been seized even if it should later have been proven that no offence was committed. The only thing which can be done is that the suspect copies can be seized and an example or exhibit taken to court and the issue speedily disposed of. If an offence is proved to have been committed, then the matter in question is forfeited to the crown; if there is no offence, it is ordered returned to the person from whom it was seized.

But heretofore the practice has been that if there is a suspicion that there is obscene material somewhere officers of the crown have purchased one or two copies which they use as exhibits which, after examining them, they come to the conclusion are obscene. Then a complaint was sworn out and an arrest made. If guilt was proven after trial was held the merchandise or obscene literature was ordered destroyed or removed from circulation; but here the destruction and the removal as well as prejudice is caused in advance-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The destruction is certainly not caused in advance, and I suggest there is no prejudice caused in advance either because there is no charge laid. It is a proceeding in rem without prejudice to the individual.

Surely the minister realizes that once you have walked in and practised a seizure in the same way as you would practise it after guilt had been proven, you are practising seizure before guilt is proven. It is true it is provisional, I realize that. I also realize it is done for the purpose of expedition; but a great deal of injustice can result from changing the procedure from a seizure after conviction to a seizure before conviction. If guilt is not proven, even though you return the merchandise afterwards, the magazine, or whatever it is, may be out of date and the store may have suffered serious financial loss.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps I might point out to my hon. friend that it would be perfectly open, without this clause at all, under the present law for a police officer to go into a store with a search warrant and seize, and then bring a prosecution on the basis of the article seized. We are really providing nothing different here except that it will make it possible to dispose of the issue without laying a charge against the individual.

The clause in the first paragraph speaks of copies which are kept for sale or distribution in premises within the jurisdiction of the court. Then the magistrate is called upon to render an opinion as to whether or not the material is obscene. It
Criminal Code
really becomes just a matter of opinion. Can the minister not realize that a judge in one province will come to one conclusion and another judge in another province having the very same material before him reach a different conclusion? I would go further than that; for example, a judge in the city of Montreal who has jurisdiction in the district of Montreal may come to a different opinion on the very same exhibit laid before him from a judge elsewhere in the province of Quebec.
It happens every day.
Yes, it does happen every day, but here we are dealing with obscene literature. What does the minister suggest is the remedy to make this uniform right across the country?

Appeal.
