Mr. Chairman, may I address a few remarks to the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl).
The hon. member has referred to the situation which might develop if a denunciation under oath was drawn up against an individual who might have bad literature in his possession. He also expressed amazement at finding this section, as worded, does not provide any recourse against a person who would unfairly denounce some other person or lay an unfair charge against someone. By reason of what has been his calling for many years, the hon. member for Cartier knows very well that civil law does not maintain criminal law and that, at any time, any person feeling prejudiced by a baseless accusation or charge would always have as provided by civil law the possibility of appealing to the provincial courts, whether there be a provision to this effect in the Criminal Code or not.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanau-diere (Mr. Paul) and those of the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) with regard to criminal intent.
I am convinced that with regard to obscene literature, the Minister of Justice has sought to make it harder to commit the offence. If I refer to clause 150 of the Criminal Code in its present form, I find that a distinction is made between the person who prints obscene literature and the person who sells it.
Whereas the printer cannot plead justification or ignorance, the seller can prove or invoke some excuse.
Now, Mr. Chairman, who provides the publicity and promotes the propagation of obscene literature?
I believe the main source of that publicity to be newspaper and magazine vendors.

Criminal Code
I am sure that if those who carry on this business were a little more closely checked, they would be more careful about buying this or that publication, no matter who the publishers or distributors might be. When those people are charged, they usually say in court: "Your Honour, I did not intentionally sell obscene literature; I sell those books by the hundreds and I cannot normally read all the books I have in stock."
I believe that, if the Minister of Justice had wanted to make the act more effective, by reaching those who are responsible for the distribution among the public of obscene literature, he should have been more severe towards the vendors of such publications, because he surely knows that printers or wholesale distributors of obscene literature do not operate in the open. There are not a great many of them but, unfortunately, they operate in various ways that enable them to circumvent the law. Distributors and vendors of obscene literature are almost invariably acquitted because of the plea that they did not know what was in such a book.
Then, Mr. Chairman, if the Minister of Justice had wanted to make the act stricter and really do something to eliminate those evil publications, he could have removed, for instance, from subsection 2 of section 150, the words:
(Text):
-who knowingly, without lawful justification or excuse.
That is where the fault lies. There is the source of the faults we have on account of obscene literature, because if you are looking for the printers or publishers you will never find them, or if you find them once they will start in another part of the province or in another part of the country.
I think the minister has taken a step forward but we humbly suggest it is not the step which he promised to take publicly in the province of Quebec in the presence of thousands of people. He promised to stop this obscene literature from being distributed all over the country, and I think the Minister of Justice would have been more well received had he included in the second paragraph the words "who are knowingly, without lawful justification or excuse". I am saying that in subsection 6 of section 150 it is clearly stated:
Where an accused is charged with an offence under subsection (1) the fact that the accused was

ignorant of the nature or presence of the matter, picture, model, phonograph record, crime comic or other thing by means or in relation to which the offence was committed is not a defence to the charge.
This means that an accused is denied the defence of saying: I did not know about it, or I had a lawful excuse, or I had justification.
I have brought these observations to the Minister of Justice and hope that he will really commence to have this obscene literature swept from the newsstands, from the stores and even from private persons who distribute it in backyards. I think he has to get at the real source, those who are really responsible for this obscene literature, and I do not know why the government is allowing such latitude to printers and publishers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to, first of all, correct what was said by the hon. gentleman. He said that I promised as Minister of Justice to stop the distribution of obscene literature across this country. I made no such promise, because I knew it does not lie within my power to do so. I promised to bring in legislation which will give the law enforcement officers effective means to prevent the sale and distribution of this literature, and I believe we have done that.
Having corrected the hon. gentleman's misinterpretation of what I promised, I should like to say that I think he has a point which does deserve consideration in connection with whether or not the publisher himself must foe proven to have had knowledge of the contents and the nature of the publication. We did consider whether we should make any new provisions with respect to this proof of intent or anything having to do with the nature of degree of guilt, but we felt that rather than deal with that which can only be to some extent on an empirical and hypothetical basis the best thing was to adopt the new procedure embodied in clause 12 of this bill under which this material could be seized wherever it was found, whether in the hands of the printer, the publisher, or the vendor, and then the issue of whether or not it is obscene may be tried and disposed of without any reference to knowledge on the part of the person in whose possession it was found. Having been adjudged offensive, then, of course, if it continued to be sold the person responsible would be liable to prosecution and conviction because he could not then claim he did not know it was obscene.

Subsection 5 of the present article 150 of the Criminal Code reads:
For the purposes of this section the motives of an accused are irrelevant.
Might that give the latitude which the hon. member for St. Denis has suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I do not think so, once there had been an adjudication under the proposed new procedure that the publication in question was obscene.

Mr. Chairman, with reference to subclause 2 I should like to ask the minister what would happen if the judge neglected to issue the summons? In the event of a seven-day delay, would the merchandise be restored to the person? It sometimes happens.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would think they would have to start the proceedings over again, issue a new warrant and make sure the judge did issue the summons in time.

Mr. Chairman, I feel we should do something more than we are doing to avoid discrimination against people who might be subject to unlawful seizures. The emphasis is on speed and under this clause action has to be taken within seven days. That is not too bad, I suppose, because the period is not longer than a week in which these books would be either restored or destroyed. In the case of an appeal, however, that would be a much longer and more costly procedure which could have extremely serious consequences for the person concerned.
It is quite conceivable, as my friend the hon. member for Cartier pointed out, that within the seven-day period two separate seizures may be made in two separate provinces. In one province the magistrate may decide that it is not obscene and it may be restored. In the other province the magistrate may make the opposite decision and have the goods destroyed. The burden is then imposed on the person who has been charged to appeal his case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But it might work the other way. The attorney general in the province where the verdict went against him may decide to appeal. This, however, is something that happens all the time under the Criminal Code under the system of law we have in Canada. There is nothing that I can see we can do about it here unless parliament and the provinces should decide to amend the constitution with regard to that question of the administration of the criminal law. Until that happens, the provinces are responsible
Criminal Code
for the administration of the law and different courts in different provinces may continue to give different verdicts under much the same set of facts and circumstances. That is why we have the Supreme Court of Canada, so that in important cases we can get one final definitive decision laying down what is the law of Canada.
But the trouble with appeals is that they cost money. Justice then depends on a person having a big pocketbook. That is something we should try to avoid.

After listening to some of the comments made this afternoon I should like to indicate to the committee that the amendment before us does not make it obligatory that the forfeited matter be adjudicated as obscene within seven days. A judge may find himself extremely busy for three months and the matter would be under consideration for that period. I have heard many comments to the effect that this is expeditious and that in seven days the matter would be heard but it is not so provided in this amendment.
I should like from the minister a clear answer as to the meaning of subclause 4 under which an order is made declaring the matter forfeited to Her Majesty in right of the province in which the proceedings take place for disposal as the attorney general may elect. I notice that different words are used. Subclause 4 refers to "matter", but subclause 7 makes reference to "copies of a publication". The same words are not used. If five copies of a publication on a newsstand are found to be obscene by a magistrate I fail to see that this involves forfeiture of all the copies of that publication throughout the entire province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry if my hon. friend misunderstood me. I never said that an order made in that case would automatically result in the forfeiting of all copies of that publication throughout the province. What I said was that it would provide an immediate and ready method whereby the law enforcement officers could bring to the attention of all vendors the fact that there had been an adjudication with respect to a publication and that they had better withdraw if from publication, and that if this warning were disregarded further prosecutions in individual cases would be permitted without the necessity of going through the proceedings in rem as contemplated under clause 12 of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I think we should give further consideration to what I should like to call this innovation of showing cause. This is something that is really foreign to our criminal law.

Criminal Code

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is not at all foreign, Mr. Chairman. There are several examples of it in the Criminal Code at the present time, to which I have already referred.
That the burden is shifted to the accused?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, there is no shifting of the burden. I thought that my hon. friend was referring to the seizure in advance of adjudication. I apologize for having interrupted.

I am speaking of the accused being summoned into court to show cause that what he did was not an offence. Basically that is something new in our criminal law. The United States system of law depends to a large extent on the show cause principle. Perhaps it is effective and desirable but because it is something new to us I think we should devote more time to it.
Under the English system of law on which our own is based the accused is not deemed guilty until he is proven guilty. I should like to hear further comments from the minister concerning reasons which justify the introduction of a new concept into our Criminal Code. I am rather disturbed by it. Once we open the door in this legislation we run the risk of undermining our concept of British criminal law whereby every person is deemed innocent until proven guilty and an accused is not forced to step into the box to prove that he is not guilty.
Of course the minister knows full well that an accused charged with a criminal offence cannot be compelled to step into a witness box to offer evidence. Here we are somewhat distorting that concept by providing that an accused must step into the box and offer some explanation. He must show cause that what he did was not a crime. This is a new concept which parliament should consider most carefully before introducing it into our system of government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has completely misapprehended the nature of these proceedings. I say again there is no foundation for this allegation that the onus of proof is shifted from the crown to the person in whose possession the goods are found.
In the first place there has to be an information upon affidavit to such an extent that a judge becomes reasonably satisfied that there is cause to believe that a publication complained of is obscene. To that extent the crown has initially to make a case. There is an onus on the crown that it has to discharge. The crown must show the judge that there is reasonable cause to believe that this publication is offensive. If the crown

does discharge that onus of preliminary satisfying the judge to this effect, the judge then makes an order or issues a warrant for the seizure of the material. The material is then brought into the court. There is the crown's case. The crown must first provide preliminary satisfaction to a judge that there is reasonable doubt to believe that there is an offence, and then the article claimed to constitute the offence is brought into the court and placed before the judge. Then, the crown has to present its case if it wishes to argue on the material, but there is also evidence presented by the crown to prove its case in discharge of the onus of the crown in these two ways that I have described.
What would happen if we did not say that the person should be summoned to show cause? We might come to, then, what right would a person have in whose premises the articles were found, what right would we have unless he was served with some sort of summons calling upon him to come in and in effect enter his defence? That does not mean in the first proceedings that the person concerned has to come into court and prove that there is no offence. He is only called upon to show cause when the crown has discharged these two preliminary onuses, the onuses which are imposed upon it in the first place, so that there is no question. It is a complete misapprehension to say that the onus of proof is shifted to the person. All that is done here is to give the person concerned the right to come in and answer the crown's case.

The minister surely recalls and knows that we have rules of procedure even in our criminal courts. This is a new procedure by which a person is summoned into court on a summons by a judge and is not accused.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.
I do not know under what section of our criminal procedure that is permissible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is the only new part of this provision. The only new principle established is that we are providing for a procedure in rem, and in order to get the person concerned into court we have resorted to a show cause summons which has been in the United Kingdom procedure for many years; but I say there is no new principle introduced beyond that. We have not introduced the principle that the person concerned must answer the case before the crown has established a prima facie case. The crown has to discharge two onuses of proof by way of satisfying the court before this person

is called upon to speak to the court at all. Therefore, there is no shifting here. It is true we have resorted to a new procedure to get the person into court. That is the only new principle. Instead of charging him and getting him into court, we serve him with a show cause summons and get him into court that way and I do not think there is any prejudice of the individual whatsoever.

I do not want the minister to be under the impression that I am opposing the procedure; I just want to understand it. I think we all want to understand what is the procedure here. The summons is laid, because the minister speaks of the crown making a prima facie case by producing what he considers to be obscene literature. After he produces it and lays it before the judge the judge on oath issues the warrant. The minister says that that is a prima facie case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: One.

At the present time when a prima facie case is made nothing else happens but the so-called accused is ordered to stand trial. But there is certain procedure at the preliminary hearing at which the prima facie case is made. The accused does not have to step into the box. That is quite different, as I see it, and he cannot show cause in any other way except by taking an oath. I do not know whether the hearing will be a new form of preliminary hearing that will be held, but there has to be some machinery set up by which he will show cause. The only way in which he can do that is to step into the box, take an oath and attempt to show cause. That, I say, is prejudicial to the person who may have been accused because if he does not succeed in showing cause he will have given evidence; there will be a deposition taken which will certainly be used against him afterwards at trial if he is sent for trial. That is the different concept that I see that disturbs me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, again I think my hon. friend misconceives the nature of the proceedings. There is no accused here; there is no accused person who has to step into the box and give any evidence whatsoever.
But he will be an accused later.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No; he will not have given any evidence that can be used against him at a trial later if he becomes accused. The cause he shows would consist of argument; he is not in the box to give evidence in the sense of an accused person giving evidence in his own behalf; for there is no accused here. If I might strain the simile, the
66968-9-352
Criminal Code
accused is the publication. There is an allegation made that the publication is obscene. It is recognized that the vendor, whoever the person is on whose premises it is found, has an interest in establishing that it is not obscene and therefore he is given the opportunity of coming into court, if he wishes, to argue that it is not obscene. He is not giving evidence in his own behalf which may be held against him if later on he should become an accused and tried. Remember this, too, that the prosecutions with respect to a publication adjudged to be obscene in the new procedure can only take place subsequently with the consent of the attorney general of that province. I suggest to my hon. friend that there is complete protection against such a malicious attempt to use anything that was said in an inquiry of this nature against the person who might later be accused.
As I see this scheme developing, if this person accepts the adjudication-he may or may not appeal-when the matter is finally disposed of, if he withdraws it from publication, makes no further attempt to publish or to sell it, I cannot see the attorney general authorizing the prosecution at all. If he wanted to prosecute him he would prosecute him in the first instance rather than resort to the procedure of disposing of the matter in rem.
I do not know whether I have satisfied my hon. friend or not. I do not think I can make it any clearer. I can only state as a fact that there is no accused; that the crown does have in two ways to make out a prima facie case. Therefore, it has two obligations on it, first, to satisfy the judge that there is a reasonable case for believing that here is an obscene publication; second, producing the publication in court by way of evidence; and, I would think in almost every case, a third obligation, namely to enter some argument before the judge who would feel that the case had been finally established. Only after these things are done, at least the first two of them, is there any case at all for a person on whose premises the matter was found to come in and answer it? I see no application of my hon. friend's argument at all.

Because this is an innovation I should like to ask the minister to allow me to examine it from another standpoint. Let us assume that someone has been brought into court because of literature that was seized on his premises. He has to show cause that it is not obscene. What will he first proceed to do? He will first offer his own opinion. He will then invite experts, specialists, sociologists, and offer all this evidence to

Criminal Code
the court that the literature is not obscene. He is showing cause. His own word will not be sufficient. He may differ from the judge's opinion and it is the opinion of the judge against the opinion of the man before him. He wants to show cause and he will show cause by bringing to bear on the court all the opinions, all the knowledge, all the information, in an attempt to show that this is art, that this is science, that this is something else, that it is not obscene. Now, let us assume that that is completed and the judge is not impressed. He thinks it is obscene and he he orders a complaint laid.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There will be no complaint laid. The only order the judge can make then is for the forfeiture of the material.

That is, confiscation. The complaint is subsequently ordered by the attorney general, or whoever it will be, if the court is of the opinion that it is obscene. In some form a complaint will be laid against him. He then comes to trial.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I make it clear that it does not automatically follow that the charge will be laid. The charge can only be laid when the attorney general consents.

I said that. Assume now the attorney general has ordered that the charge be laid and the man ultimately comes to trial-now, he is the accused-what more at trial can the accused do? What more evidence can he offer than he offered at the time he was called upon to show cause? He has no time to prove, as the result of expert evidence, that it is not obscene. He has attempted to do that at the time he was called upon to show cause. He will then have exposed any defence he may have had on the show cause procedure. There are certain procedures at the trial which protect him. For instance, at trial, he may not go into the witness box but on a show cause procedure he may step into the witness box and he may say things in the show cause procedure which he might be protected from saying at a trial.

With respect, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the hon. member for Cartier has missed the whole point of this legislation. We all agree that we want to clean up this obscene literature. The only dispute is upon the method of doing it. I feel that the minister has brought forth a provision which is going to do the job very well.
The trouble with section 150, as it is now, is that it requires a prosecution against an individual. People were reluctant to bring charges against the merchants who were selling these magazines. Normally, when a charge was brought, a merchant would 
come into court to defend himself, not because he wanted to protect the literature, but to defend his own name because he did not want to be branded in the community as a person selling literature of this type. Now we have a section which will allow the municipal authorities to go out and gather up literature that is salacious, and not the proper type to be circulated in the community, without the storekeeper being charged. This section will help to eliminate the opposition of the merchant, who will not come into court and battle to protect his name because his name is not before the court.
As far as this "show cause" summons is concerned, the show cause summons is an important part of the section. I say that because I have seen the advantages of the show cause summons in general law practice. It is familiar in probate court procedures, for example, where a show cause summons is issued when it is not expected that persons summoned will appear. For instance, in the closing of an estate a citation is issued to the heirs, legatees, creditors and so on to inform them of the closing and to invite them to come in and show cause why the estate should not be closed. If they do not show up, then they have no cause for complaint. The minister has brought into use the show cause summons in this legislation so that the merchant will not have to defend himself as a person distributing salacious literature but, in his absence, the magistrate or judge can adjudicate on the matter and if so warranted, order the material destroyed.
There is another very good point about this section so far as I am concerned, and that is that no charge can be brought except with the consent of the attorney general. This provides that the merchant will not be personally charged as a result of the evidence brought forth without the consent of the attorney general, and therefore the merchant is not so likely to come in to fight each case. As the hon. member well knows, the problem so far in connection with cleaning up this indecent literature in any town has been that wherever the municipal officers try to prosecute a man they have the usual difficulty in securing convictions because magistrates do not like to adjudicate on matters where their decisions will reflect upon the reputations of men who are otherwise well regarded in the district. I think the show cause summons is an important part of this legislation in that the man himself is not upon trial but only the literature. The man, therefore, is not going to come forward to do battle to protect his name and thereby hinder literature clean-up efforts.

I believe this is a provision whereby we are going to be able to clean up the obscene literature in the nation, and that there is no other system of doing it. The show cause summons is part of this system. I think we have to keep it, so that a magistrate or judge can come to a conclusion that literature is obscene without charging anyone. Further the owner of the bookshop or newsstand is not worried about his good name being taken away as a result of publicity on a criminal conviction because his name does not come into it. Only the magazine comes into it, and he is probably not interested in the magazine. This is a big step forward that we are taking, and I believe it will permit us to erase this literature from the nation. We could not do this under section 150, but we can do it under this section. We should not weaken the amendment by taking out of it the very things that make it vital, and able to do the job we want it to do.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) will perhaps admit that the only power conferred to the judge under the proposed amendment is that of deciding whether the publication is obscene or not. If the literature, or publication, is considered obscene, the judge immediately advises the alleged guilty person and within seven days, that person has to prove that the literature is not obscene. Now, this literature may be obscene; but, being legally in possession of it, the vendor may claim that he was unaware of the fact. Under this amendment, that person will have to appear in court and will only be able to plead one thing: "The publication is not obscene", but, will not have the right to prove non-awareness with regard to possession of such literature or to any other legal plea.
Consequently, the case of anybody really in possession of a publication and who has the right to sell and distribute it, will go before the attorney general and will be prosecuted. Consequently the difference is that while formerly, the obscene literature could not be seized, whereas under this amendment, it can be so. Therefore, why have two prosecutions when a single one would be appropriate? If the publication is proved obscene, nothing prevents the Minister of Justice from prosecuting, and all the indicted person may say is that the literature is not of obscene character or that the accused was unwittingly in possession of it.
Thus, the procedure would follow the English practice, which has always been applied in Canada, i.e. that the accused is presumed 66968-9-3524
Criminal Code
innocent until proven guilty. Now, this principle would be saved and the amendment introduced by the Minister of Justice would have its full effect if the confiscation of the publication were simply permitted and immediately followed by the prosecution.
To my mind, such proceedings, by which the accused or the alleged accused may be summoned to show cause or move that his publication is not obscene become superfluous. Besides, everything is the plain consequence of a statement by one person before a judge, saying: "Here is an obscene publication". The judge, recognizing it to be so, then calls the vendor within seven days in order to prove that the publication is not obscene. That is all the law provides.
The crown prosecutor or crown attorney, is not informed of that procedure. Now, we must not forget that if all this handicaps the accused it may also be unfavourable to the crown because the crown lacks the necessary evidence that the literature is indeed obscene.
As the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) said, the accused may ask for a hearing of experts and attempt to prove that the said literature is not obscene, while the crown is not there to help the judge decide if the publication is so or not.
I consider this a step forward by the minister, but otherwise he knocks at the wrong door and, though the legislation presents some progress, it is a very small step forward. For that reason, we will nevertheless support the proposed amendment, because it is better to have half a loaf than none.

clarify one point in his reply to the hon. member for Cartier. Suppose that a warrant has been issued under subsection 1 of section 150A and that the court has been satisfied that the publication is obscene. The attorney general institutes-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And that there are reasonable grounds for believing it is obscene.
Yes. Then the attorney general decides to take proceedings. Will the evidence given before the court under subsection 4 serve in the proceedings instituted by the attorney general.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No; 1 do not believe so. In fact, I think it is quite clear that the proceedings before the judge under the proposed section 150A would not be admissible in evidence in a criminal prosecution for the same publication at a later stage. These are entirely new

Criminal Code
proceedings. They would have to be commenced de novo, I would think. As I think I have said this before, a court of concurrent jurisdiction, however, would regard the reasons for judgment in the proceedings in rem as of very real authority in reaching a decision on the question only of whether or not the publication complained of is obscene. But so far as the question of whether the accused has had this article in his possession is concerned, whether he offered it for sale and all those matters which are purely evidentiary matters, the evidence, if any, given in the proceedings in rem would definitely not be admissible in evidence in any criminal proceedings.

That is exactly the reason why I have asked that question of the Minister of Justice because I noticed in his reply to the hon. member for Cartier he said that this evidence would not serve. But it is not included in this new clause of the bill. I am just wondering whether, not being included, that evidence would not serve.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am satisfied that you do not need any provision. I am satisfied that the present provision of the law is clear. Here you have two entirely different proceedings. They are not different stages of the same proceedings. They are entirely different proceedings. In the earlier proceedings in rem, as I understand it, there was no accused before the court to give evidence which might be admissible against him later on. I am satisfied that the present rules of evidence and the present procedural rules would clearly establish that these are two different things and that the proceedings in one are not admissible in the proceedings of another.
That would be another matter for discussion among lawyers.

Mr. Chairman, it might be convenient for the committee if I were to pass on to subclause 2 of clause 12 which is section 150B. However, I do not want to cut short any other hon. member who may have questions on the clause. I feel that when we come to this clause, we find something that is certainly most amazing in its form and in the manner in which it will change "criminal guilt" in our country. Inasmuch as I am absolutely opposed to and see a grave crime in the tied sales mentioned in the explanatory note, I feel that the matter can be handled justly only in either of two ways, neither of which is the manner in which it is stated that it will be handled. In order to convict a person of a crime of trying or purporting to make a tied sale so called I think the Minister of Justice should have a good deal of courage and ban tied

sales in the matters of publication and ipso facto it would be a crime in this country to try to sell literature in the manner of tied sales.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have done so.

If he fails to have that courage to ban tied sales, he should then apply only just methods. If this clause is construed, here is the manner in which the Minister of Justice intends to bar tied sales. They are not barred automatically. I say it should be done automatically. I say that he should bar tied sales in publication matters.
What is a tied sale?

It is explained in the note if the hon. member would read it. A tied sale is where a person will say, "I want to buy these five magazines" and the other person says, "I will only sell you these five magazines if you buy these too". That is a tied sale.

Any
magazine or just obscene magazines?

No; any magazine. Then comes the matter of obscenity after that has occurred. Then a man is convicted of a crime according to this amendment, if the person to whom a tied sale is offered is apprehensive only that the literature may be obscene. This is a fair comment. It amounts to the position wherein I lay a charge of theft against somebody, he goes to court and proves that he did not steal it but still is found guilty because I thought he did. That is what this section says. It says that everyone commits an offence who refuses to sell a certain number of magazines-unless he sells them to a person-and he is found guilty if the other person is only apprehensive that the literature may be obscene. I say to bar tied sales absolutely in matters of publication or else, if you are going to do something else, you have to do it according to justice and not permit a man to hide behind the fact that he may have thought that the other two were obscene, go to court and show that they are not obscene and the man be found guilty of a crime that he has never committed.
That is the position in which this section places citizens in this country and it amounts to the example I have given where a person may lay a charge of theft against somebody and then that person is acquitted-and properly acquitted-but still he is found guilty because the other man thought he did it. That is section 150B. I am sure the Minister of Justice will admit that. Although I am absolutely opposed to tied sales, I think it is a great crime to be in that situation. If you wish to do so in matters of publication,

bar all tied sales. If you do not do that, at least you must do it justly and not put one citizen in a position where he is found guilty of a crime if the other person only thinks he is guilty.

The minister allayed our fears somewhat about this show cause clause and putting the burden of proof on the offender when he pointed out to us that when the crown had to prepare a case, first somebody had to provide information on oath. First, somebody had to provide information on oath and then the judge had to be satisfied that there were grounds for confiscating the book. Then the person concerned, the vendor, is summoned to show cause. The minister's argument will be considerably weakened if the vendor has to appear before the same judge because this judge has already tried the case and given judgment. So that the vendor is placed in the position of persuading the judge to reverse his judgment, and certainly if he is to show cause he should be summoned before another judge, not before one who has already tried the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In that case without question the judge would feel he was biased and would withdraw, and make certain another judge or magistrate tried the case.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond thought perhaps I had missed the point of this clause. I want to assure him that I am just as anxious to provide the machinery to clean up this obscene literature in our country as is he or any other hon. member of the committee. I am afraid it was not I who missed the point of the debate, it was he. We are discussing an innovation in our law, and if it is a proper innovation we will deal with it. But the question of showing cause I fear a little because of the element of there being the possibility of a person being placed in double jeopardy. His case is tried on its merits before one judge under the show cause procedure that it is not obscene; the court does not agree with him, and later through the intervention of the attorney general a complaint is laid. He is then summoned before another court and he must again prove that the material is not obscene. He is being placed in double jeopardy there. He is being tried twice, and that is a thing we should try to avoid. In the province of Quebec we do not have to show cause in civil matters as in the other provinces; but we are dealing with a criminal matter, and that is something I am really concerned about. If there is no double jeopardy here, even in a minor form, I do not agree. The fact is that a person or his literature in
Criminal Code
question is being tried twice-of that there is no doubt-and it is something which is foreign to our Criminal Code.
On the other hand, I would draw to the minister's attention that a court under subclause 8 means, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, a judge of the superior court. Whether it is a judge of the superior court sitting in criminal matters or whether it is a judge of the superior court sitting in civil matters, I do not know. Our judges in the province of Quebec sit in civil matters unless they are especially delegated to sit in a criminal matter.
Now, assume a person is summoned before a judge of the superior court to show cause. Then he is summoned before another court, not before a judge of the superior court, but a criminal court. Here he is exposed to difficulties. I submit that whilst there is anxiety to provide legislation or machinery in our law to deal with obscene literature, let us not jump out of the frying pan into the fire. Let us not in an attempt to clean up one thing create another danger, which may be a very serious one. I would like the minister's explanation with regard to subclause 8 of clause 12 in which a court is defined as a judge of the superior court in the province of Quebec.
Then if a case is to be met and the person summoned does not succeed in showing cause, he will be transferred to another court, which is a criminal court. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know quite how I can explain any more clearly than I have. In the first place, there is no question of double jeopardy, because no one is placed in jeopardy in the proceedings in rem at all by any stretch of the imagination. We have further provided that with respect to the publication adjudged to be obscene by these proceedings in rem no prosecution against any individual on a charge of selling that publication in that province shall be launched without the consent of the attorney general. Therefore no one can even be placed in jeopardy once unless the attorney general thinks it is a proper case, or for such reason as, for instance, the vendor, notwithstanding the adjudication that it was obscene, did continue to sell it instead of withdrawing it from circulation. So only if the attorney general consents can anyone be placed in jeopardy, and then under the amendments that we have introduced he will be placed in jeopardy for the first and only time.

Criminal Code
There is no question of transferring anybody to another court or transferring the proceedings to another court. I have said, and I say again, that these are two entirely distinct, separate and non-related proceedings. One is an inquiry in rem to adjudicate upon the merits of the issue: Is or is not a publication obscene? The other, if a prosecution is instituted, is an ordinary criminal prosecution started in the ordinary courts where such prosecutions are made, in which an accused, for the first time accused, is placed in jeopardy for the first time. The proceedings before the court which were the in rem proceedings are not admissible in the criminal court where the accused is charged.
I cannot make it any clearer than that. I only hope my hon. friend, if he is not satisfied with my explanation, will say so because we cannot get any closer together, and I am afraid the only course open to him then would be to express his dissatisfaction by voting against the clause.

No, it is not a question of voting for or against it; we all want to attain the same objective. Let me illustrate what I mean. A man is suspected of having stolen goods in his possession. A search warrant is ordered and the police seize the stolen goods and bring them to headquarters. There they are identified by the owners as their property. Then the accused is told, "Now, sir, we have prima facie evidence that you are in possession of stolen goods; come and show cause that you have the right to hold that stolen merchandise." The minister will at once admit that under our system of criminal law, if he is called upon to show cause there he is really placed in a very serious and prejudicial position. I only give that as an illustration to indicate that this show cause provision is foreign to our law. It may not be in other jurisdictions in other countries, but it is foreign to our law. It may be a good system, and it may be desirable, but we should be convinced that it is desirable or we should debate with great caution before we vote on it.
Is the hon. member of the opinion that this section requires a man to show cause or just invites him? He does not have to show up, you know.
He does not have to show up but he will have himself condemned by his absence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He will not be condemned; the magazine will be condemned.

The fact that the hon. member rose was the first intimation I had that members were concerned about this clause, because this amendment is as good as all the other amendments we are proposing to the Criminal Code.
Perhaps I might be permitted on this clause, Mr. Chairman, to give an explanation of clause 31, which is related to clause 27, the one immediately before the committee. These two clauses amend the law so as to make provision for the giving of time for the payment of fines. The present state of the law is that, first, where a fine is imposed for an indictable offence there is no provision for the giving of time and, second, where a fine is imposed for a summary conviction offence subsection 3 of section 694 authorizes the court to direct that the fine shall be paid forthwith or, if the accused is unable to pay forthwith, at such time and on such terms as the summary conviction court may fix.
What is proposed by clauses 27 and 31 may be summed up very briefly as follows: The law on this subject is to be made the same for indictable offences as for summary conviction offences. A duty is to be imposed on the sentencing court to satisfy itself that the convicted person has the means to pay a fine before sending him to prison for failure to pay. The objective of these amendments is to eliminate, so far as our criminal law is concerned, to the greatest extent possible any remnant of imprisonment for debt. We hope that the result of the amendment will be that imprisonment for failure to pay a fine will only occur where there has been a contempt of court, that is a failure by the convicted person to pay a fine ordered by the court even though he has the means to pay it.
In the result it is anticipated that the state will benefit morally, economically and socially by a decrease in the number of persons who would otherwise be started on a career of crime by reason of prison associations, that is that they have been sent to jail because they were unable to pay their fines, and that the state will also benefit financially by an increase in receipts from fines and a

Criminal Code
decrease in the prison population with a resultant decrease in the expense of maintenance of prisons.
I should perhaps remind the committee that this is not the first time this change has been advocated in this house. It was advocated by the Prime Minister on a number of occasions when he was a member of the opposition, and specifically it was advocated by him in 1956 when he introduced a bill which would have had the effect of amending the Criminal Code. This bill was No. 167 of 1956 and, although not in exactly the same terms as the proposal now before us, it was certainly to the same effect. I should remind the committee also that this proposal was advocated by the Fauteux committee report, and that there is similar legislation in the United Kingdom. The general experience with legislation of this kind has been that, far from encouraging the commission of crime, it has been calculated to produce the result that instead of having people sent to jail simply because they did not have the money to pay their fines they are kept out of jail and thus the association of those persons with hardened criminals is reduced, with consequent benefit to the whole of society.

I should like to point out to the committee that on July 1, during the debate which took place on that day, the word "flight" in clause 3 raised for examination many of the ramifications of the drafting process that do not ordinarily come to notice outside the mind and office of the draughtsman.
In subsection (1) of the proposed section 5A reference is made to an aircraft "in flight" and to the termination of a "flight" of an aircraft. In this context, no definition or other aid to the interpretation of either "flight" or "in flight" is required. Obviously "flight" has the primary dictionary meaning of "act... of flying or moving through the air" and "in flight" means in the act of flying or moving through the air. No definition is required to make it clear that "flight" is not used in any of the many other dictionary senses of the word such as, for example, "running away" or any of the other modern senses such as, for example, the designation of a scheduled trip of a commercial airline

Any such sense is clearly inapplicable. Most words in the English language have several senses. Where the appropriate one for a word used in a statute is dictated by the context, it would be unnecessarily cumbersome to spell it out by a definition.
In the proposed section 5A of the code the function of subsection (4) is not to designate the sense in which the word "flight" is used. It was on the contrary, inserted to extend for the purpose of the provision the meaning of "flight" in its ordinary sense of the act of flying or moving through the air by adding on to that act, the act of taxiing at each end of the true flight. To accomplish this, subsection (4) was worded as follows:
(4) For purposes of this section and paragraph (3) of section 2 an aircraft shall be deemed in flight from the moment the aircraft first moves under its own power for the purpose of taking off until the moment it comes to rest at the end of its flight and when it so comes to rest that flight shall be deemed to have terminated.
So worded I do not think any person reading subsection (4) with subsection (1) could fairly misinterpret its effect and I do not think any court after proper argument could misinterpret its effect. However, that, taken by itself, can be misconstrued, as established by the debate that has taken place.
The point that bothered some hon. members, justifiably, I think, can be eliminated by deleting the words "at the end of its flight" in lines 27 and 28 so that the subsection would read:
(4) For purposes of this section and paragraph (30) of section 2 an aircraft shall be deemed in flight from the moment the aircraft first moves under its own power for the purpose of taking off until the moment it comes to rest and when it so comes to rest that flight shall be deemed to have terminated.
However, as was made to appear by one hon. member at the end of the debate-I think it was the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo-this would completely distort the whole concept in the ordinary case of a takeoff by terminating the "flight" when the aircraft comes to rest at the end of the runway to wait for clearance from the tower. This experience, I may say, is instructive and underlines the danger involved in making amendments on the floor of the house.
Various alternative suggestions occurred to us, with regard to which I do not think I need go into detail, in an endeavour to meet all the possibilities, and I should like to ask leave of the committee to withdraw the amendment now before us and to substitute therefor the following:
That clause 3 be amended by striking out lines 24 to 29, both inclusive, on page 2 and substituting therefor the following:
(4) For the purposes of this section and paragraph

(30) of section 2, "flight" means the act of flying or moving through the air and, where an aircraft has been in flight, the flight shall be deemed to have commenced when the aircraft first moved under its own power for the purpose of taking off and to have terminated when the aircraft ceased to be in motion.
That, it seems to me, would cover the case both of the movement for the purpose of talking off and the other related but distant case of the aircraft which comes to rest in Canada at the end of a flight, as we attempted to define it, though not at the end of the so-called scheduled flight. We have taken care of that, I think, by the use of the words "to have terminated when the aircraft ceases to be in motion". Mr. Speaker, I say that the coal industry in Canada is still in a serious plight. The next decade promises to be a critical period for the coal industry. The provincial minister concerned in Nova Scotia has broadly described the position, and if we have raised the question in this house it is because it is imperative that every effort be made to try to maintain this industry in operation in the forthcoming years. I must say that the only means now available is to grant subsidies. It is a temporary remedy, but it will have to be continued in order to maintain at least the major mines in operation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I at this time express my views on this matter once again, and say what should be done to pull the coal industry out of its present predicament.
First, greater use of coal in the maritimes themselves should be encouraged by every possible means. That is where greater use of coal is to be expected in the future, and action must be taken so that residual petroleum products, which are threatening to replace coal, will not have an opportunity to do so.
Secondy, an effort should also be made in eastern Canada, in Newfoundland for instance, and in the province of Quebec, as well as in eastern Ontario.
Third, every possible effort should be made to increase sales of Nova Scotia coal in Ontario centres.

To achieve the above purposes, I think we should resort to the following means- and when I say we I mean coal producers, the federal government and the provincial governments as well. Progress should be made in the mechanization of mines, for the simple reason that if no attention is paid to mechanization, coal production not only will remain at its present level, but it will decrease, because production costs will be too high.
In 1958, at a meeting of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, the chairman of the dominion coal board made the following statement:
Machines must be installed, and if you will allow me time, I shall explain the matter in my own terms, without going into too many technical details. Otherwise, I shall yield the floor to Mr. Ignatieff who once a year, makes a survey of the progress achieved in the field of mechanization and developments. Incidentally, his report of last year is quite favourable, encouraging and accurate. Mechanization is achieved in a proportion of about two thirds, but its benefits are not up to two thirds of the value. It is the last third that will enable us to see if the aim has actually been reached. Perhaps I should illustrate my remarks by way of an example. At the present time 60 per cent mechanization will give a 50 per cent yield but 95 or 100 per cent mechanization should yield from 80 to 90 per cent. Therefore, the true increase of efficiency will depend on the next third of mechanization, which includes the coal-dressing apparatus as well as various other machines which have just been developed.
Mr. Speaker, that is how we realize that mechanization must be quickened as soon as possible to give a yield of at least 80 to 90 per cent.
Now, we should also improve the quality of coal-that is the producers should get organized to provide the consumers with a purer and better dressed product.
Moreover, if possible, we should facilitate and modernize the transportation and handling facilities of coal.
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important matter and I know that at this stage of the study of the bill, it may not be proper to insist on those points. However, I wanted to put my own point of view on record and, as the hon. member for Gloucester said last week, we are in favour of the adoption of this legislation and we hope that it will be approved as soon as possible.
We also hope that the companies concerned will come and submit their plans to the dominion coal board. Besides, I hope that those companies will mechanize their mines


as quickly as possible. I hope that, through this bill, the government will make loans to those companies to enable them to speed up mechanization.
I am rather surprised to note that the amounts made available for mechanization are raised only to $20 million. I believe that it should have been brought up to $30 million. However, the hon. minister indicated to us that if the companies would come here and submit larger plans, the government would study them and that they would probably be favourably received. That attitude is encouraging, not only to the coal producers of Nova Scotia, but also to those whose living depends on that industry.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we support this bill and we hope that it will be used in the best possible way.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few brief comments in connection with this bill. First of all, let me say that we support the principle of the bill as being a short and timid step in the right direction; and that direction is recognition by this government of the fact that the economic health and welfare of the coal industry is a national problem. We are pleased to note that that is indicated in the bill by the extension of the application of this act to all coal producers in Canada for the obtaining of assistance in the modernization of their plant, equipment, machinery processing and so *n. But the bill itself has limited application even in that respect because the major concern of the coal companies in Canada at the present time is markets. While this bill will assist in more efficient production and possibly will lower costs in some respects, it does not provide the markets which are necessary in order to keep the mines operating.
I was greatly interested to hear the minister make reference to a study being undertaken in connection with the coal industry in Canada. We shall look forward with great interest to the result of that study.
I cannot deal with this subject without thinking of a small city in southeastern British Columbia which has suffered severely in recent years. It does not happen to be in my constituency; it is in Kootenay East. However, I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. McFarlane) would support my remarks in this respect. I refer to

the city of Fernie which has suffered severely in the last year or so because of the closing of a large coal mine which had been in operation there for over fifty years. From our point of view some of these companies show a lack of a sense of responsibility in view of the advantages they have enjoyed throughout the years as a result of their operations in Canada. Here is a company engaged in a successful operation and a profitable one.
The mine I am speaking of is very close to Fernie, and the workers for the most part live in Fernie and have done so for over 50 years. But it is completely United States owned. They have not closed the mine because they are losing money in the Crowsnest pass coal mines as a whole; they closed the Fernie mine because by so doing they will maintain their rate of profit. They can maintain their profit by keeping their other mine operating in the Crowsnest pass. There is no consideration for investment by the province or the municipality in the development of the city, public services, streets, hospitals, schools and all that sort of thing. There is no concern for the workers directly concerned. This coal mine was closed on, I think, about a week's notice, being given to the council of the city of Fernie after all these years of operation at a good rate of profit. I might also mention, Mr. Speaker, that this company has received very generous consideration throughout the years from the government of British Columbia.
It creates a situation, as it were overnight, where there is unemployment and a lowering of values of properties within the district because of lack of demand for houses, and need for certain facilities; it also entails a lowering of the value of investments on the part of the province, on the part of the municipality, and on the part of the workers concerned in connection with their homes.
It is the opinion of the members of this group, on behalf of whom I am speaking this evening, that it is not good enough in this age to allow companies to act in what we consider to be a completely irresponsible way so far as recognizing their responsibility to the province, the municipality and to the people directly concerned. What are we going to do about it?
In our opinion, we will never overcome this type of situation unless we have a national policy, first of all, with respect to the development of coal mining and the marketing

We are quite convinced that over a period of time, with the right spirit, there can be developed a national coal policy which will change this situation into one where the owners and the workers concerned will be at least assured of a measure of security and reasonable remuneration.

I think we should be assured that the $6,500,000 is going to be enough to modernize the other mines in Canada along with the $4,500,000 and the allowances that this bill makes. I have no objection to that at all. I think this bill is necessary. If we are going to pass this amendment to take care only of some of the problems of the Dominion Coal Company, then I think there is no need to change the name or to give the impression

Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act that this is a very important bill. We must be assured that there is enough money.
I think it is absolutely necessary for the minister and his department to supply the facilities of his department in technical research and whatever is involved in the technical part of the department so that assistance can be given to many of the operators who are now finding it impossible to continue operations. This is true in Alberta and in Saskatchewan and it certainly is true in British Columbia, and it is proved by the fact that a number of the mines are closed down. I think we would still like an answer to some of these questions, so may I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOAN, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if we could not complete this bill tonight? We would be quite prepared to go ahead.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOAN, ETC.
speechtext: May I say that if the minister will indicate how, in any little way, this will help British Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan, we might be prepared to let this go.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOAN, ETC.
speechtext: That is the very question I raised, and I associate myself with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I think we all want to co-operate in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not very easy to tell in advance what may happen in three, four or five years. Representations have been made to the dominion coal board by different companies in the west, and at the same time we have this application from the Dominion Coal Company. The board has calculated that the amount of $10 million would meet the applications we expect in the next few years, maybe one, two, three or five years at the most. We cannot foresee events and give the details of what might happen next year or the year after.
We are presenting a bill for $10 million. This application of the Dominion Coal Company has not been decided. We know this is the maximum that can be granted, and that is all we can say at the present time. Who can tell what the situation will be in so far as coal is concerned within the next year or two? We are doing whatever is possible. The dominion coal board is studying the whole case. They have their officials looking over the matter in the western provinces and in the maritime provinces. We are doing our best. We ask for $10 million additional and will try to meet the requirements at the present time.

May I say that the committee should be satisfied with the explanation I am giving. I am very frank with the committee in giving this, and very sincere.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOAN, ETC.
speechtext: The minister is referring to a regional problem. Certainly we are all very sympathetic to this problem. The minister, I am sure, would be willing to make it known to the committee that if a similar situation existed elsewhere on a specific basis he would use his best offices to do as he has done in this case and provide some assistance for that situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOAN, ETC.
speechtext: That is exactly what we intend to do.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION, INCREASING AMOUNTS OF LOAN, ETC.
speechtext:
May I say this: The minister has asked for money under this amendment, and while we are not averse to that if this will help the coal mining enterprises in the maritimes, at the same time he is making a pretense that this will help the coal mining enterprises all over the Dominion of Canada. He has not yet presented any evidence whatever that this will help the coal mining enterprises in British Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan. Therefore, may I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.
